subtopic: PRESERVATION OF ARCTIC WILDLIFE
PRESERVATION OF ARCTIC WILDLIFE
speechtext: Are any steps being taken to prevent extinction of various forms of Arctic wildlife, particularly the polar bear, as a result of unrestricted hunting made possible by modem development of snowmobiles and air transport and, if so. what are they?

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PRESERVATION OF ARCTIC WILDLIFE
speechtext:
1. I am informed by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories as follows: Yes. Three important species of Arctic wildlife, muskoxen, caribou and polar bear, have been declared by the governor in council to be species in danger of extinction. The muskox has been protected from hunting by legislation since 1917. Only male caribou over one year of 23033-451
age may be hunted in the Northwest Territories east of the Mackenzie river, and caribou meat fit for human consumption must not be wasted. Female polar bears with cubs under one year of age are protected throughout the Northwest Territories except Banks island, Victoria island and the Mackenzie District. Under the Northwest Territories game ordinance and regulations no persons are permitted to hunt game from an aircraft or from a motor vehicle. Furthermore, only Indians, Eskimos and a very limited number of white trappers with historic rights are permitted to hunt and trap wildlife in most regions of the Northwest Territories. Further legislation to provide additional protection for polar bears and other Arctic wildlife is now under consideration.

subtopic: EXPO '67-EMPLOYMENT OF STUDENTS
EXPO '67-EMPLOYMENT OF STUDENTS
speechtext: Will any students at the university and high school level be employed at Expo '67 and, if so (a) how many (b) in what capacities is it intended that these students will be employed (c) from what regions of the country will these students be drawn (d) will preference be given to any particular students on the basis of region or language?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: EXPO '67-EMPLOYMENT OF STUDENTS
speechtext:
(a) The corporation and other employers on the site of the exhibition will employ students at the university and high school levels providing these students meet the employment criteria established for the positions in which they wish to be employed. As there are no classes of employment specifically reserved for students and as the criteria to be met vary widely, it is difficult to determine the number of students that will be employed. However, it is presently estimated that the corporation will employ some 650 students and the concessionaires a further 2,300. In addition, it is estimated that some 300 students may be employed by the exhibitors in supporting type services.
(b)	Certain students may be employed in skilled capacities such as translators or interpreters. However, the vast majority will be employed in semi-skilled and unskilled capacities such as: entrance attendants, parking attendants, ushers, maintenance men, hostesses, guides, clerks, cleaners, information agents, protective agents, platform guards, typists, identification officers, gardeners, ride attendants, area representatives, ship attendants, messengers, waiters, restaurant help.
(c)	A program for the recruitment of a special category of personnel comprising 225 hostesses and 30 male guides, geographically representative of Canada as a whole, has been planned and is being implemented to greet visitors to the exhibition.
(d)	No preference will be given on the basis of regional origin insofar as this is feasible. The corporation will attempt to recruit students or other employees on a national basis. Ability to speak more than one language will be considered an asset in view of the international character of the exhibition.

subtopic: STEPS TAKEN FOLLOWING U.S. BOMBING OF NORTH VIET NAM CITIES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STEPS TAKEN FOLLOWING U.S. BOMBING OF NORTH VIET NAM CITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I
asked the Prime Minister whether the government would look favourably on the request that some day this week we be given an opportunity in this house to discuss the Viet Nam situation. While there has been no answer in that regard as yet and no opportunity to debate this matter, there are a number of questions that I should like to place before the Prime Minister at this time.
Over the week end or within the last few days the President of the United States said in Omaha that one should count ten before dissenting from United States policy in Viet Nam. I ask the Prime Minister, in view of the expansion of bombing that has quite fearful, dark and ominous dimensions and the possibility of a world war, whether the government of Canada has directly endeavoured to exert its moral influence upon the United States to exercise a degree of restraint in expanding the bombing operations; and whether any steps have been taken in the last few days that would indicate that the North Vietnamese are prepared in any way to allow for the convening of a conference so that this ever increasing and frightening threat to world peace might have some hope of being removed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STEPS TAKEN FOLLOWING U.S. BOMBING OF NORTH VIET NAM CITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the first half of my right hon. friend's question, the possibility of a discussion of this matter in the house before any recess is being considered by myself and my colleagues. One possible way of arranging for a debate would be when interim supply is requested; but we will be discussing this matter tomorrow morning at a cabinet meeting.
So far as other questions are concerned, our position on the matter of the bombing of North Viet Nam has been made clear to the United States government recently, indeed over the week end. I said in the house that we regretted the extension of the bombing, and that remains our position. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I think no government has pressed harder for an end to hostilities in Viet Nam by negotiation than this government, and we will perhaps continue so to press.
DEBATES	7123
Inquiries of the Ministry
Perhaps I may be permitted, because of the seriousness of the question, to repeat what I said publicly on May 1:
There seems to me to be one overriding consideration here; not who is responsible for what, but how can the fighting and the slaughter and the suffering be ended and the people of that distressed land be allowed to live their lives in peace and freedom in a political society of their own choice without outside interference in making that choice, and outside pressures after the choice has been made.
I then went on to say, and this remains my view:
The first concrete step in this direction would be a cease fire, or a more formal armistice agreement, put into effect as part of a wider pattern of peace negotiations without prior conditions.
Once the cease fire was in effect and as negotiations progressed, equivalent and phased withdrawals from South Viet Nam by North Viet Nam and by the forces of other governments could take place under international supervision.
I can only reiterate, Mr. Speaker, the hope that a cease fire can be arranged which would bring an end not only to bombing from the air but also to shooting on the ground, and that negotiations can begin. I sincerely hope that with negotiations under way the process of phased withdrawal on both sides could begin.

subtopic: STEPS TAKEN FOLLOWING U.S. BOMBING OF NORTH VIET NAM CITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, has there been any reaction to the visitation by Mr. Chester Ronning which would indicate that the North Vietnamese have any feeling or attitude of mind that might lead the right hon. gentleman to believe there is any hope at the moment of a conference being convened?

speechtext: It is impossible to be optimistic at the moment in regard to an early convening of any such conference. However, while it is impossible to be optimistic, it would be most regrettable if we ceased in any way to work for such a conference. That remains our policy.

speechtext:
On a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, in view of the widespread concern that has been expressed by prominent world figures such as Senator Robert Kennedy, does the Prime Minister not consider that the United States would be more fully seized of the gravity of the situation if the Canadian government formally expressed disapproval of the escalation of the war by the bombing of the Hanoi and Haiphong areas?

subtopic: STEPS TAKEN FOLLOWING U.S. BOMBING OF NORTH VIET NAM CITIES
speechtext: This government, with the support of the house I am sure, is engaged in a continuing process of trying to bring about negotiations. Because of our position on the international truce commission, and because we have been able to enlist the services of a very experienced negotiator in these matters, and in the midst of an effort to bring about negotiations, I do not think, Mr. Speaker, it would be desirable for me to comment any more than is required on the policies of either side in this dispute. We have already indicated our regret at the extension of the bombing, and I prefer to leave it at that at this moment.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, June 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mac-Eachen for the second reading of Bill No. C-207, to authorize the making of contributions by Canada toward the cost of programs for the provision of assistance and welfare services to and in respect of persons in need.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as this legislation is concerned, it has been made perfectly clear by various speakers in Her Majesty's loyal opposition that we support the measure in question, though believing there are various changes which should be carried out to make these proposals more effective.
We are greatly disappointed at the absence of any suggestion on the part of the government that an additional $25 a month is to be made available to the old age pensioners of Canada. No one can argue that today, with the cost of living the highest in history, $75 a month meets the elementary requirements of fairness or equity. There are many thousands of people who have been waiting for action, and who from week to week live on a mere pittance, their hopes kept alive by periodic statements that sometime, some where, some place, something will be done.
Today, I intend to review the stand which we, as the opposition, have taken on this matter throughout the last couple of years. I make no apology for going into detail, and I resent very much the suggestion of the minister that there has been on the part of the opposition an attitude of filibustering this bill. As far as the Conservative party is concerned, representatives from all the provinces, I think, have made their views clear. They have the right and duty to do this.

The minister in a moment of annoyance, I think, decided he would brand the opposition as being responsible for a filibuster, thereby taking the pressure off the government for action on behalf of the old age pensioners. Just after he spoke the other evening in this regard I decided to look up the meaning of "filibuster". In the old days in parliament speeches of seven, eight, nine or ten hours were not unusual. Those days, of course, are past. I recall I used to get Hansard in 1910. I was greatly impressed by a member by the name of Mr. Lafortune who, at the end of 14 hours, told the Speaker that he was "about to come to the essential portion" of his argument.
I recall very well that in the days of Prime Minister Mackenzie King speeches on occasion were of almost limitless extent. No one suggested that Mr. King would engage in a filibuster against himself and his party. Mention is sometimes made here of Senator Wayne Morse in the United States. I find that on one occasion he spoke for 22 hours and 26 minutes; he was excelled in length only by a member of the legislature of Texas who spoke for 28 hours and 30 minutes.
Filibusters are in the nature of speeches made without any objective in mind except to hold up the passage of legislation by the government. It is not a filibuster to demand from the government justice on behalf of the old age pensioners of Canada.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
The charge of filibustering has no effect, but it indicates a state of mind. The minister and the government do not like to hear this question discussed. They seem to be oblivious to the fact that everywhere across Canada there is an almost universal demand for this action to be taken.
The expectation last week was that the house would adjourn by Friday for a summer vacation. I have heard of no further prophecy since that prophecy turned out to be at variance with the facts. However, I believe the time has come for this house to determine on regular adjournment periods-at Christmas time, at Easter and for the summer vacation.
In the United Kingdom they have regular adjournment periods. I think we might very well follow that course; for in the last couple of days the government has seen fit to add one or two further measures to those already before the house.
July 4, 1966

[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
And so it goes. Always at the end of a session governments find that there are matters they would like to get cleared away. The result is indefinite postponement of the rights of hon. members. Those who are here, not those who are travelling abroad, have the right to look forward to a reasonable expectation of being able to meet with their constituents and enjoying the rest they have earned by being here for such a long period of time.
Somebody suggested to me that one of the reasons for general expectation of an adjournment on last Thursday was that Mr. Commissioner Spence had his report ready and wanted to go on vacation. But now apparently the report is not to come until after adjournment. I do not want to see the commissioner denied his anticipated holiday. I would suggest, if the report is ready as is generally believed to be the case, having been completed some weeks ago, that we would be prepared to have the report brought down while the house is in session rather than waiting indefinitely for it.

speechtext: Order, please. I would therefore take the liberty of reminding the right hon. gentleman that at the first opportunity he should address himself to the bill now before the house.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was simply pointing out that the house was to have adjourned last Thursday but that now the adjournment is indefinitely postponed, that various matters have been brought in at the last moment by the government and that we are prepared to have one more brought in. That was the point I was endeavouring to make by way of introduction, as you expressed it, to a full discussion of the bill before the house. I thought that the government would welcome the suggestion that we are prepared to wait even longer if only it will bring in the report instead of setting it aside to be brought in after the session adjourns.
It has been interesting to follow the government's peregrinations in connection with old age pensions. During the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) said that he would not do anything that could possibly be construed as endeavouring to buy
Canada Assistance Plan votes. That was the way in which he met the perfectly responsible program that we advanced for assisting the old age pensioners of Canada. As recently as June 14, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) reviewed the matter that is now before the house. But there was not one word of hope for the old age pensioner at that time.
What happened between June 14 and today? There have been no unusual cataclysms. The rise in the cost of living has been at about the same rate as previously. What has caused the sudden interest of reputable reporters in the press gallery, who have been able to set out in some detail the announcement that the minister will make when he has the opportunity to speak? The minister has had many opportunities to speak. Any day on motions, before the question period, he can get up and let the old age pensioners in on the secret.
He has not done so. On Thursday he put up the attractive member for Westmorland (Mrs. Rideout) who made a delightful speech. If everyone were as attractive as she is the house would be a most attractive place. But I was attracted by the fact that she did not give any of the answers. She could have told the expectantly waiting country what the government is going to do. But no, her lips were sealed except with regard to those matters on which none of us is in disagreement.
What has brought about this change? There was no thought of it on June 14. I do not know what has happened, but the press reports that the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon), a member to be reckoned with-the government has been reckoning with him for a long while-has urged the government to implement the Croll plan to provide a guaranteed income to old people.
The press also reports that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) believes the government should make the Croll plan part of its program. The press reports that the hon. member for York North (Mr. Addison), a man who understands the needs of people, allegedly accused the government of lying on this matter. I presume that had reference to its recumbency. Finally, the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Whelan) was reported as saying that unless something was done he could not face his constituents.
I do not know whether these press reports are correct. If they are, they indicate that

July 4, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan there is a basic reason for the sudden conversion of the government to the need of taking action. Long before June 14 the Senate report was published. Why has there not been any action on it until now in the last hours before adjournment? First the government said it would not do anything about increasing the old age pension from $75 to $100. The suggestion of such an increase was ridiculed by the Prime Minister when he spoke in Prince Edward Island. He said he was not going to make an auction block out of a political campaign. He was not going to promise $105. It is interesting that that is the figure he mentioned.
Since that time the government has had every opportunity to act but it has not acted. Every Liberal member has voted against increasing the old age pension from $75 to $100 a month. When I hear some members of the Social Credit party speaking out I am reminded that they joined with the Liberals in that action. Had it not been for that fine, filial relationship between the Liberal party and the Social Credit party, the old age pensioners of Canada would today be getting $100 a month. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) is not in the chamber. If he were I would refer him to some of his own contributions in this connection when on almost every occasion we tried to get action, he was almost the first to rise to argue that our amendments were not constitutional according to parliamentary authority. He rushed in on every occasion, but in his absence I refrain from going into details.
From the beginning to the end on this question, not only in this session but in previous sessions, the government has revealed itself as playing a game, a charade of hypocrisy, wherein the old people of Canada are to be engaged in guessing the meaning of the words and the promises made by the government. What is the reason for this change of attitude? This is a government that bends and, if the wind is strong enough, it is always able to bring about that which it previously had said could not be done. It always stands firm until public opinion is aroused.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
What do we find in this connection? The minister has been denied an opportunity to open what one might refer to as Pandora's box. I think this is unfair to him. I might as well tell the house what he will say when he speaks because it has been made available in the press over and over again. Several days
tMr. Diefenbaker.]
ago representatives of the Toronto Telegram and the Toronto Star stated that when the minister spoke he would indicate that nothing is going to be done now, but that assistance will be given in the fall by the provision of an additional $30 per month to qualified pensioners. Mind you, the minister did not give the information, but the newpapers indicate that this information comes from well-authenticated sources which have always been reliable in the past.
Again I can only rely on these formidable witnesses of the press who have stated that anyone whose income is below $1,260 per year will be given assistance. What will happen is that a needs test plus a means test will be applied so far as the needy of this nation are concerned. How many are there in this category? Outside of the farming community there were 425,446 in 1961 who had an income of under $1,000 a year. That relates to total income which means that the $65 per month that was being received was included. We had raised their pensions to that amount by then. How many people fall within the category of $1,000 to $2,000 in income, again including the $65 a month? In that category in the same year there were 158,501.
During the last election campaign, and here in this house, we took the stand that the tremendous exactions under the old age pension scheme would permit an increase being provided out of the surplus moneys collected over and above the actual expected requirement. The hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) was able to find out as a result of questions, that as of March 31, 1966 the excess that had been collected amounted to approximately $217 million. As of December 31, 1965, the amount was about $140 million. In other words, in three months there was an increase of $77 million. At that rate of increase the amount today over and above what is actually needed for the payment of old age pensions would be in the neighbourhood of $300 million.
I should like to ask the government a few questions and perhaps the Prime Minister will answer them. Can he inform the house whether or not it is a fact that the surplus to which I have made reference has been judged by the experts of the Department of Finance to be sufficient that it would be feasible for old age pensions to be increased immediately to $100 per month? Will the Prime Minister indicate that those experts have gone even further and have come to the conclusion that
July 4, 1966

the surplus would permit an increase in pensions to $125 a month by next year? Following the increase in 1963 of payments into the old age security fund, 1 per cent additional to raise them from 3 per cent to 4 per cent, is it a fact that experts in the Department of Finance calculated that by the fall of 1967 it would be possible to make an increase not only to $100 per month but to $125 per month?
These are things about which we are entitled to have some information. The surplus next year will be much larger than it is this year. I should like to know why the government will not take action, except by way of a smoke screen provision to be announced, on behalf of all the old age pensioners of this nation.
I have made reference to the Prime Minister's speech in Charlottetown on October 16, 1965. In this regard I should like to quote from an article written by Mr. Fraser Kelly which appeared in the Toronto Telegram on October 18, 1965. Mr. Speaker, similarly to everyone in the house I want to say something about the subject of old age pensions. Before I do that, however, I want to express my own disappointment at the bill as a whole. If the minister were to rise and ask me whether I intend to vote for the bill my answer to him would still be in the affirmative. Those of us who want improvements in the field of social welfare have frequently been faced with suggestions which appear to be half a loaf while they are only a quarter of a loaf, and in such circumstances we are forced to support this bill rather than have nothing at all.
First of all I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that it seems to me that our attitude to welfare has over the years always been one of charity. I have found that private charity has carried over into the public domain. Every time persons in need have required assistance they have been able to obtain it only by begging from the municipal or provincial authorities, by having to prove need or by having to go through some kind of humiliating test.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The improvement in this legislation, and it is supposed to be an improvement, about which the minister has boasted is that instead of having what has been called a means test there will now be a needs test. The only difference that I can see is, as someone has said, in the spelling. Instead of having to prove a certain amount of income the person seeking relief, in addition to showing what his resources are, will have to show what his budgetary needs are. Some social welfare person from some board or department will be in a position to say to the applicant for assistance; I consider this item is necessary for you but that item is not. This is what the test means.
If a person is in necessitous circumstances some bureaucrat, someone representing some municipal or provincial department, will be able to go over that person's means of living and say to him: This you may have but this you may not have; you may not have this because in my view, and in the view of others like me, you do not need it. You do not need to smoke. You do not need to take a trip somewhere once a week. You do not need a television set because I consider it to be unnecessary.
Make no mistake about it, the needs test just as much as the means test means that the person applying for assistance will have

to humiliate himself not only by showing what his resources are but will also have to haggle with someone, to bargain with some welfare officer, when getting assistance. This is as humiliating as the means test ever was.
Of course, the minister is able to boast about an improvement because we started with an evil, wicked base, a humiliating base, and when you reduce the humiliation somewhat you are able to boast about improvement. However, the humiliation is still there to a large extent. We in our party, as our leader stated the other day, are looking forward to the day when assistance to people who require it will be based on the concept of a guaranteed annual income or some form of income maintenance. If a person's income does not add up to the level which has been set, not by some arbitrary officer somewhere but by what a budgetary analysis will make clear a person requires in order to live in decency, then his income will be augmented up to that level.

Obviously, if you have an income maintenance program, you have got to find out what income a person has; otherwise you cannot have an income maintenance program. I am sure the minister knows that as well as I do. If you are going to say, you must have at least X hundreds of dollars a year or a month in order to live and we will make up anything below that, then there has to be some kind of measurement of a person's income. There are two ways of measuring it, however. One would be to put the person concerned through some humiliating test where every detail has to be discussed, as is the case with the needs test.
I realize that many people have said the needs test is an improvement. I know that most social workers have said that the test the minister proposes in the plan under discussion is an improvement. I have no doubt it is an improvement if you have a good social worker. A good social worker, if he or she has a heart and a knowledge of the needs of people, will be able to get more for the person concerned under this kind of plan than he or she could under the categorical payment plan. I realize that. However, I say that the requirement that a person sit down and haggle with someone else over what he is entitled to have before he will be able to get assistance does not make me any happier. This is a humiliating thing, and I do not like it any more than the minister, I am sure, likes it.

Mr. Speaker, how does the minister know? He is taking me to my second
Canada Assistance Plan point. This is the second major weakness in his plan. He sets no standards and he does not know what the studies will reveal. He has no idea what the standards will be. Furthermore, anyone who knows anything about social welfare in Canada, and I do not pose as an expert, knows quite well that standards differ from province to province and from community to community within a province. The standards will be different for metropolitan Toronto and the larger cities in this province compared with the smaller communities in which there may be no social welfare staff and where some committee of the council will set up what the standards shall be. So long as the council has to bear some share of the payment, then the council will be concerned with the cost and the applicant for assistance from the council will suffer.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
This takes me to the second major weakness of this bill. However, may I first get back to the point I was making earlier. There are two ways of testing an individual's income. One is the humiliating way and the other is the simple way in which all of us are tested for income tax purposes. The part of the Senate committee report which, if I understood it correctly, appealed to me was the suggestion of an income calculation which would be as simple as the income tax form, or perhaps not as simple but as clear and as limited in the information required as any income tax form. To that extent it would be an improvement.
I come back then to the lack of standards in this bill. This worried me immensely from the very start, and I must say that I have not been able to feel even as approving of the bill as some other members in this house, even some of those who have criticized it.
The one great evil in this country over the years, the one heartbreaking fact about Canada which I am sure has been the cause of greater disunity than anything else, language and culture included, has been the terrible inequality which exists in this country. I have been in communities in this country-and I am not going to mention even the provinces, let alone the names of such communities-where the welfare program is absolutely shameful. There is a lack of welfare workers and a lack of any humanity toward the people who are in need.
These communities will be able to get 50 per cent of their expenditures in an indirect way through the provinces, no doubt, but will

July 4, 1968
Canada Assistance Plan their programs be improved? Is there any guarantee that they will treat the needy of Canada with greater consideration than they have up until now? Furthermore, there are provinces in this country-and the minister represents a constituency in one of them -which with the best intent in the world cannot provide the assistance to the needy in the province that anyone with any compassion would consider half adequate, let alone sufficient.
As far as I can see, and I am sure I see correctly, this bill does nothing to establish standards across Canada. It leaves it entirely to the provinces to establish those standards. If the minister says that this is because of the constitutional situation, then I would say to him, with the greatest respect, that the constitution is used too much as an excuse for refusing to equalize the opportunities in this country. Without claiming to be a constitutional expert, but as a lawyer who has read something about our constitution, I know of nothing in the constitution which would prevent the minister from providing in this bill that if such and such a standard were met the government would pay 50 per cent, if such and such a standard were met the government would pay 60 per cent, and if such and such a standard were met the government would pay 75 per cent.
I make the concrete suggestion that there ought to be in the bill an inducement to improve the standard of care for the needy people in Canada, so that those provinces which cannot afford the standard that some other province is able to afford will gain from the bill a great deal more than is now offered them. Until such time as we do get in this country, Mr. Speaker, a sense of urgency as to the need to equalize opportunities for all Canadians, whether young or old, in need or in jobs, and until the big gaps in income per head of population which now exist between one province and another are eliminated, we will continue to have divisive influences which feed on the natural and desirable discontent and resentment prevalent among people in sections of the country who feel that they are not provided the same opportunities as those in other areas of the country. This is the second major weakness in this bill.
Third, another reason I feel unhappy about this bill, aside altogether from the question of the old age pensioners, is that modern welfare involves something more than the payment of money. It seems to me that this bill

ignores the progress that has been made in the concept of welfare in 1966. It is not merely a matter of giving assistance. It is not even a matter of giving assistance to train welfare workers and to provide various forms of therapy for elderly and ill people who require it. There is also the concept in modern welfare thinking of providing older people with things to do, of funds being made available so that they can live useful lives in this country, and of building environments for them so that they can lead useful and dignified lives.
The other day the parliamentary secretary to the minister stated how important it was to take care of disturbed and retarded children. It has been pointed out in some provinces, particularly in the legislature of the province of Ontario in the last number of months, that there are tens of thousands of children who are disturbed and who grow into difficult people, to put it mildly, as they grow older.
What is needed in order to meet this problem is not merely an offer to pay a little bit toward providing the kind of service outlined in this bill but large, really massive injections of capital assistance to build the homes and the institutions required and to train people to take care of these tens of thousands of youngsters across Canada. There are probably 100,000 to 200,000 young people who, because of their environment, background and for various other reasons not of their making, or indeed often not of their parents' making, if they know who their parents are, require homes, institutions and the kind of care which, as far as I have been able to study the situation with the help of one very close to me, involves the provision of one teacher or one trainer per child.
As far as I can see there is nothing in this bill that recognizes the modern approach to social welfare. When I say nothing, perhaps that is an exaggeration and I should not put it quite that strongly; but there is very little in the bill which recognizes the trends in modern welfare.
This takes me, Mr. Speaker, to the question of the old age pensioners. I did not intend originally to take part in this debate, and I must say that the person who more than any other got me to my feet was the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), to whom I will return a little later.
Listening to the debate on old age pensions and how much we should give our old age pensioners, I felt-and I am sure every other
July 4. 1966

hon. member including the minister must have felt this way-as if we were in a kind of Alice in Wonderland atmosphere. I am sure it would be most unjust to the minister, to all his colleagues in the cabinet and to the members who surround him to suggest that they have any less concern for the needs of our old people than have we on this side of the house. I am not saying this with tongue in cheek. I am sure that the minister is a kindly man-he looks it and I hope looks are not deceptive-who is as concerned about the plight of the old people in Canada as is anyone on this side of the house. However, he and his colleagues and those who support him have been the victims of an attitude over the years. They are the victims of an attitude which objectively, whatever their hearts say, is an attitude of callousness and mathematical calculation.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
If, Mr. Speaker, you look at the history of the old age pension in Canada you will find, I think, a sordid story. Perhaps you will forgive me if I review the dates and a few facts. We start in 1927, after a long fight by the late J. S. Woodsworth, with a pension of $20 a month with a means test. I must say that every time I look at these dates I feel humiliated at having been in this country when this kind of thing happened. From 1927 until about 1944 people aged 70 and over received $20 a month after a means test. In 1943 or 1944 it was up to $25. I learned a long time ago when I was studying a little economics that if you make your base low enough your increase, no matter how small, can be a very large proportion of your base. Therefore, when you start with a measly, niggardly, inhuman amount of $20 a month with a means test and you raise it to $25, you of course have raised the amount by 25 per cent and everybody pats himself on the back for having been generous.
In 1946 the amount was raised to $30 a month but still with a means test. In 1948 it was raised to $40 a month, still with a means test. Without going back to the economics books, Mr. Speaker, I venture to say that the $40 in 1948 was worth not one cent more than $20 was in 1927, if it was worth even that much.
Not until January 1, 1952, which is the effective date, was the means test removed. The $40 was left. The $40 figure remained all the time from 1948 to 1957, despite the immense increase in the cost of living created by the Korean war in 1951, 1952 and 1953.
Canada Assistance Plan The increases in the price index were greater than any other we have known since the end of the second world war. Yet we left the old age pension at $40 even though it was without a means test in the fifties. We introduced old age assistance at age 65.
The aged were fortunate that there was a series of elections following one another in rapid succession. Thus in 1957 the St. Laurent government increased the pension by $6 to $46. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition formed a government-

The point I wish to make, and I should like it to sink in if I can make my point vigorously and sensibly enough, is that at no time has there been the suggestion that the amount paid to the old age pensioner is enough. What there has been is a rather shameful kind of haggling-raise the amount by this or raise it so much. We have had political parties doing what we are doing here, namely, haggling with each other. Should the pension be $75? Should it be $100? Should it be $90? The fact is that even $100 is not enough for those people who have only the old age pension to live in dignity and self-respect. The Canada Assistance Plan will still have to be used for aged people living on a $100 pension.
Like other hon. members, Mr. Speaker, I have received letters from various people about this old age pension matter. What struck my fancy and my heart, if I may say so, even more than any letter I received, is one letter which I read in the Toronto Telegram of Monday, May 9. In the Telegram there is a column entitled: "Ask the Tely". In that column there is the following moving question by an old age pensioner, and it is all

the more moving because of its simplicity than anything else:
Is there a good second hand clothing store in Toronto. I'm an old age pensioner, and find it hard to pay the price asked for new clothes.-O.A.P.
Then the Telegram gives him the answer, referring him to three or four stores where this old age pensioner could get second hand clothing.
I lower my voice deliberately, Mr. Speaker. I say that so long as there is one person who is forced to write this kind of note to a newspaper in a society as rich as Canada, with a government that boasts of its concern for humanity and for welfare-so long as this happens every member of this house ought to be ashamed of the job parliament has failed to do for the old age pensioners of Canada. Whenever one reads this sort of thing in the newspapers of this country, and I have just referred to a mild complaint, a mild request, and remembers that the gross national product has gone up tremendously in the last number of years, I think that the citizens of this country, particularly those who have the means to live with self-respect and decency, ought to be ashamed of their failure to provide for these people.
I have in my hands a letter from an old lady:
I am a widow 70 years old. I have only got my $75 old age pension to live on. I find it very hard with every thing so dear and things always going up.
This is the sentence to which I particularly want to refer:
I wonder if there is any way you could help me.
Aside from any personal assistance, the way I can help her is the way all other hon. members of this party have decided to help her. That way is by raising this issue with all the force at our command so that this government will yield and bring about some humane treatment of the old people in this country. If somebody wants to call this a filibuster, let him do so; let him misuse words and twist the motives and intentions of people.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The fact is that the Social Planning Council of Toronto has pointed out that an elderly person needs $138.96 a month in order to live in some decency. If that sum were brought in line with the present level of the cost of living it would need to be increased somewhat. What we are saying to the minister and to the government is not that $100 a month is
July 4, 1966

enough for the old age pensioner-I am sure no one, even on the other side of the house, believes it is-but that it is essential as an act of humanity to increase the universal pension to $100 a month in order that those who still require assistance under the Canada Assistance Plan may be fewer in number and so that fewer people will be humiliated by having to submit to some test or other.
I am sorry the Minister of Transport is not here. I am sure he has other things to do. I am not blaming him for not being here, but this is my opportunity to speak and I cannot wait for him to be here. But the other day the minister interrupted the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) to say, as reported in Hansard at page 7065:
Yes, sir, I will be very proud to say that no country in the world makes such generous provision for its old people as does Canada. Everyone in this house knows it, and the hypocrisy over there is not going to conceal it either.
The ignorance of the minister, displayed with typical Pickersgillian assurance, is really shameful. When a minister of the Crown makes a statement of that kind to the house with the self-assurance which my friend of long standing used the other day, it cannot help but arouse the ire of anyone who knows a little about these things.
I do not intend to quote large numbers of statistics, but I hold in my hand a report provided by the research and statistics section of the Canadian Department of National Health and Welfare. This is not something compiled outside Canada; it is provided by the minister's own department. The date is January, 1965. Let me draw attention to several interesting figures. The report deals with various social security items in five countries, Australia, Canada, Great Britain, New Zealand and the United States. It appears that these five countries were chosen because there is greater similarity in their general approach to social security questions than might have been expected had other countries been chosen as well.
Look at the first table on page 2 of this report. It gives government expenditures on health and social welfare as a percentage of the gross national product in those five countries. Canada comes third. There are two countries below us on this list, the United States with 7 per cent, and Australia with 8.2 per cent. The Canadian percentage is 9.4. However, in the United Kingdom it is 10.5 and in New Zealand, 12.1. I should have said these figures are for the year 1962-63.
Canada Assistance Plan
But on the issue concerning which the Minister of Transport spoke, the issue about which he boasted, namely, the treatment of our old age pensioners, Canada comes last of those five countries. As shown in table 3 on page 5 of this report, New Zealand was spending 3.6 per cent of the gross national product in this field. In the United Kingdom the percentage was 3.4, in the United States 2.7, in Australia 2.3, and here in Canada the figure was 2 per cent. Last of the five. Yet this is the country which is supposed to treat its old age pensioners much better than any other country. This is what the Minister of Transport dares to say. And if anyone wonders what is included in these expenditures footnote (e) at the bottom of the page makes it clear that they comprise old age security benefits and old age assistance payments. So it is the total payments to the old people that are involved. Canada comes last in this series of five countries.
Is there any reason for this? Is our standard of living, or gross national product per capita, lower than that of New Zealand or Australia or the United Kingdom? I appreciate that Australia and some other countries in the world have had old age pensions for a much longer time than we have and that in many instances the payments are more analogous to those under our Canada Pension Plan than they are to the old age security payments. A number of us in this house do, I am sure, regret that we did not begin the Canada Pension Plan at age 65 many years ago so that many of the problems we now face would not have arisen.
I was not a member of this parliament when the Canada Pension Plan was passed, but as I read the Canada Pension Plan and the speeches made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare during the election campaign and since, it seems to me that the Canada Pension Plan took the universal payment under the Old Age Security Act into consideration in arriving at the terms of the scheme.
Obviously, no one intended that the maximum of $104 a month, if I remember correctly, was sufficient for a person to live on. Time and time again spokesmen for the government said: When we have both the Canada Pension Plan and the old age security scheme in operation people will be able to breathe more freely than they can now.

No one can suggest that even in 1966, let alone in 1975, it is possible for anyone to live anything but a shabby restricted, undignified and crushing existence on such an amount. Why all this long argument with the minister? Why is the government so adamant about this? Why is it that instead of coming forward with an obvious minimum of justice for the old age pensioner the government is considering plans, as the newspapers suggest, which include a means test, a needs test or some other tests, and all of this to be promised for the fall? Why not now? If hon. gentlemen opposite mean what they have said, if they intend to be recognized as a government of heart concerned about the Canadian people, who more deserve this concern than the older people and why not introduce now the small measure of justice which is represented by an increase to $100 a month?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak in support of the Canada Assistance Plan and, because I do support it, I wish it to pass promptly and therefore will be brief. As most members in all parties are aware, this plan has been strongly supported by many leading social workers in Canada, by men and women who are not much interested in grinding political axes but who have a real interest and expert knowledge in the field of social welfare.
This plan extends a bold, new guarantee to all Canadians in need. In accepting it the people of Canada for the first time accept responsibility to meet all the needs, no matter how great they may be, of Canadian children, widows, the disabled, the blind, the elderly and the unemployed. Under this plan we accept unlimited liability. We undertake to charge the public treasury to discharge our responsibilities to the needy throughout Canada. This is a program which I support and of which, as a Liberal, I am very proud.

While I support this bill, Mr. Speaker, I urge the minister to consider very seriously certain minor improvements in its administrative provisions. While the basic principle or guarantee to meet all needs covered by the bill is new, some of the administrative machinery is old and I believe can be improved. I urge that before the bill becomes law at least two administrative reforms be made by the minister. The plan now provides for an agreement between the federal government and each province and for the payment under this agreement of federal money to each province to meet the needs of its residents. This tends to make the program dependent upon the initiative of each individual province. This should be improved. The provinces may delay and in the different provinces benefits may not be based upon consistent principles.
Moreover, it seems to me unsound that the spending of money raised by federal taxation should be under the complete control of the individual provinces; nor am I convinced that the administration of this new program is best entrusted to the provincial welfare departments.
How is the problem to be met? I submit that we have sound precedents in our great universities, hospitals, charitable foundations and other public institutions supported by public funds but not directly controlled by governments. I suggest that in each province a joint Canada-provincial foundation be established, to be run by a board of governors on which the province and the federal government would have equal representation but with representation also from the ranks of labour, business, the professions and other interested community groups.
Such a foundation could also serve a very useful purpose in co-ordinating governmental efforts with the efforts of the very large number of private, charitable organizations now in the field. At the present time there is a real shortage of trained social workers and there is a great need for co-ordination of public and private effort in our war on poverty. The federal money paid each year to each such foundation could be subject to the scrutiny of parliament. Parliament would not lose financial control.
Would the provinces object on the ground that such a proposal was not discussed at the federal-provincial conference or that their welfare empire would be transferred to a public foundation? The foundation would not be federally controlled. There could be no valid objection on that ground. If the idea is
July 4, 1966
sound and welcomed by the general public, it would surely be accepted by the provinces. Nor can reforms suggested in this house be completely foreclosed by prior decisions made at federal-provincial conferences.
My second point is that it is vital, if federal money is to be spent, that we should have some say in the method by which needs are to be determined. No member here wishes to impose anything in the nature of a humiliating test: We cannot afford to have social workers, who are in short supply, checking on the needs of our citizens. On the other hand, if we are to eliminate need and poverty in Canada we must make certain that our money is spent wisely and that only those who need it get it.
Possibly we could adopt for this purpose one of the suggestions contained in the very valuable report made by the Senate committee on aging, the Croll report. Needs could be determined upon the basis of a return similar to an income tax return, with spot checks to catch the inveterate cheaters who unfortunately are to be found in some numbers in any society.
While the changes 1 have suggested are minor and administrative in nature I believe they are important. I hope they will secure the support of members of all parties in the house, of the Canadian public and, most important of all, of the minister who is responsible for this bill.

Mr. Speaker, in a few brief words I would like to support the fight that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) has consistently waged over the years for a better deal for those unable to help themselves. I think the argument he presented in his able speech this afternoon is completely unanswerable by the government, and I make a plea to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), who also represents a Nova Scotian constituency, that before the end of this debate he inveigle the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) into the house to make a statement that the request of the Leader of the Opposition is going to be met.
The most compelling and unanswerable statistic that I have found in my study of this problem is printed at the bottom of page 10 of the Anal report of the special committee of the Senate on aging. It might be assumed by a good number of Canadians that older people would have the advantage of some assistance from their families. Yet paragraph 3 of
Canada Assistance Plan this report, at the bottom of page 10, point out that in 1961 there were 570,000 of what are called unattached persons, that is, widows, widowers or older people whose children have moved out, over two-thirds of them women and that their median income on the basis of non-farm sample was $829, with 60 per cent receiving less than $1,000 annually. In an aside the report says that we know less than we should about how these people manage.
An even more compelling statistic is that of the remainder, some 252,000 persons, 63 per cent of them were women living alone or with non-relatives, and were presumably dependent for the most part on their own resources. Of this latter group 53 per cent had incomes of less than $1,000, and among those age 70 and over 47 per cent of the men and 50 per cent of the women received almost their entire incomes in the form of old age security pensions. Thus we have a figure of approximately 130,000 people with no other income than $75 per month.
It is generally accepted that one-quarter of one's income should be spent on providing a roof over one's head. But for people in this category a generous nation suggests that $18.75 or $19, not to cut it too finely, is sufficient to spend monthly on accommodation. Where is it possible to get accommodation at such a rent in Canada today?
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
It has been suggested by various members who have taken part in this debate that if we pass the Canada Assistance Plan, permitting the federal treasury to enter into partnerships with the provinces which could vary from one end of Canada to the other, we will be applying different standards to help our elderly people in need, depending upon the provinces in which they live. This is quite obvious.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) also drew our attention to the great difference in municipal welfare services across Canada. It could be pointed out that voluntary welfare services provided by agencies which exist in different parts of Canada also do not cover the whole country. We have the Red Feather appeals in metropolitan, city and town areas but no help is provided in many parts of the country by those agencies covered by the Red Feather campaigns. I think this argument tends to snowball in favour of something being done in a dramatic and even generous way by this parliament so that we



July 4, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan do not write off many members of a generation who are unable because of their age to look after themselves.
At page 11 of the Senate report to which I referred earlier there is an interesting table giving the percentages of non-farm population 70 years of age and over with annual incomes of less than $1,000, by sex, age, and marital status. Just dealing with one group, the male group, for the year ended May 31, 1961, the figure for those from 70 to 79 was 37 per cent, from 80 to 89 it was 58 per cent and for those 90 and over was 62 per cent.
One could go into the impelling needs brought about by advancing age, medical assistance and perhaps special foods. The costs of these are mounting inexorably and income is declining drastically. This situation is simply not fair to older Canadians.
Let me make a final point to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) in view of my familiarity with the area from which he comes. He represents Inverness-Richmond and Cape Breton. While prosperity there is not as noted as in other parts of Canada, the people do enjoy a reasonable environment. They have a love for things in Nova Scotia and wish to stay there to make their living. They are very proud people and I am sure if the minister went to their doors and attempted to explain a needs test as opposed to a means test he would not receive a warm welcome.
I am sure that the minister could look about the villages of his constituency and find that many of the people would sooner deprive themselves of the extra help that could be provided under a formula tied in with a test, deprive themselves of the necessities of life, rather than go through the humiliation of filling out such a form. I am sure there are hundreds of people in Inverness-Richmond who have that feeling. I know from my own mail that there are thousands in my particular area who feel that way.
In conclusion let me say that unless we wish to write off and relegate to the garbage heap of Canada tens of thousands of Canadians the minister would be well counselled to bring in the increase suggested by the Leader of the Opposition and others who have taken part in this debate.

Mr. Speaker, for the past three or four days the members of this party and, I think it is fair to say, the members of all other opposition parties have been urging the government to
[Mr. McCleave.l
reconsider the Canada Assistance Plan legislation and to bring in coincidental measures which would provide a minimum of $100 a month in old age security without a means test. During the three or four days I do not think one day has passed but that the newspapers of this country have reported that the government is considering doing something along this line. We can only hope they are right.
By way of encouraging the government and the minister to take some action in line with an increase in old age security pensions immediately I felt that for my part in this discussion I might do well to point out that it is not only old age pensioners who want and need more money and not only members of the opposition who are trying to get it for them but that some of the leading newspapers in Canada have come out almost daily repeating what we have said here. I should like to quote from one or two of these newspapers which have expressed this point of view.
The other night during this debate my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron), said that by and large it would be remarkable to find that the newspapers of Canada were urging action for better social legislation. I think that has been the general case. Quite often in the past when editorials in newspapers have been concerned with social legislation they have said: "No, no, whoa, whoa" or "go slow." At this time it is quite remarkable to find that such newspapers as the Toronto Telegram are encouraging the government to do something. Let me quote from an article in the Toronto Telegram of June 25 this year under the heading "Aged Need Help":
Canada's aged who are forced to subsist on a fixed income deserve additional government assistance. Now.
This is a matter that should not be put off any longer.
The spiraling costs of living have made it impossible for many of our old age pensioners to make ends meet. According to the cost of living index, prepared by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, it requires $1.43 today to buy what $1 did in 1949.
The article goes on to say:
The first payments under the new Canada Pension Plan will be made on Jan. 1, 1967, but these people will not benefit from it. The Canada Assistance Plan will establish what is tantamount to a means test when it is finally launched.
Not only would our aged find a means test demeaning; but by the time the assistance plan is in operation, many of them may not be around to
July 4, 1966

enjoy the additional benefits they might have received.
That is why it is essential the government consider other steps with which to help those in need.
The article then goes on to state that the government should proceed with these steps immediately and not confine itself to the proposals contained in the Canada Assistance Plan.
On the same date another Toronto newspaper, the Star, which I believe is the leading Canadian newspaper so far as circulation is concerned, had this to say about the subject we have been discussing for several days and continue to discuss this afternoon, under the heading "We Can Rescue Canada's Over-65s From Want":
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Poverty is the usual condition of Canadians over 65. According to the report of the special Senate committee on aging, 54 per cent of them had gross money incomes under $1,000 in 1961-less than $3 per day.
Compulsory retirement and unemployment keep them away from the Canadian feast of affluence which their lifetime of work helped to create. The committee found more than half of the 1.5 million Canadians over 65 to be in need of help.
How will the country, which clearly owes them dignity and comfort in their old age, give that help? The Canada Pension Plan comes too late for them. And from their standpoint, there are two things wrong with the Canada Assistance Plan which will soon be placed before parliament.
First, it will require each person to take a needs test before receiving assistance. This process will be costly and slow-and the needy aged can least afford to wait for help. Also, many Canadians of the older generation regard any kind of searching means test as humiliating, and may forgo help rather than submit to it.
The Star, like the Telegram, goes on in its editorial to urge the government and parliament to make a study of this matter and take action on the recommendation of the Senate committee on aging, which was basically a guaranteed annual income. I think we are approaching that situation and will come to a guaranteed annual income in this country. I believe this will be a very fair and efficient way of administering our social security legislation in time to come, but it is not going to help today's generation of old age pensioners. What they need, and what I think all hon. members in the house would like to see them receive, is more immediate help in addition to the proposals of the Canada Assistance Plan.
The Canada Assistance Plan has some good elements. It is good housekeeping from an administrative point of view. But the gap left by the failure to provide immediate help in a basic way to the old age pensioner is too
Canada Assistance Plan serious to be ignored by members of this house. I am very hopeful that, as has been reported by the press of Canada, the government will change its mind on this subject and bring in at an early date improved old age pension legislation. As it is now, what is happening, as my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre remarked during this debate two or three nights ago, is that the minister is saying to the old people, "We cannot do anything for you under the Canada Pension Plan because that legislation was not designed for you, and we cannot do anything for you under the Old Age Security Act because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) will not give us the money to raise the pension. Your only recourse is to fall back on social assistance and so we are providing that with the old means test re-introduced."
We in this party, as in the C.C.F. which preceded us, are quite accustomed in fighting for improved social legislation to accepting half a loaf instead of a loaf, and there have been times when we have accepted a slice rather than a half a loaf. But in this particular instance what is being asked of us and the older people in Canada is to accept not half a loaf or even a slice. We are being asked to buy the attractive wrapper that goes around this package, and I believe that many hon. members on both sides of the house do not think this is good enough.
I believe that those persons receiving the old age pension at the present time are probably the last of our Canadian generations left in the valley of scarcity. The rest of us, thanks partly to the work and sacrifices of these older people, are emerging and have emerged into the sunlight of abundance to some degree. I believe that, if for no other reason, this government, parliament and the country should activate themselves more on behalf of improving the standard of living of our senior citizens.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say I am very hopeful, from what I have read in the papers and have heard from pretty well all corners of this house in recent days, that the minister will do something in this connection and do it in the very near future.

I notice again that when we rise to speak on this side of the house a member of the government shouts "filibuster." We hear this word every so often in this chamber whenever members of the

July 4, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan opposition for one reason or another feel very strongly about a subject and insist, much to the chagrin of the government, upon an adequate examination of it. We heard this word used a year or so ago in the flag debate when my hon. friends in the official opposition felt very keenly on the subject and, at the invitation of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) himself, entered into an extensive debate. But because it did not please the members of the government it was called a filibuster.
Again today, and for the past few days, every time a member of the opposition rises, no matter what party he speaks for, to discuss the Canada Assistance Plan and more particularly the matter of the old age pensioners of this country the cry of "filibuster" is raised. Personally I do not really care whether the Liberals want to call this debate a filibuster. In this party, and I am sure in the other parties, we make no apology whatsoever for taking up the time of the house to discuss this matter. So far as I am concerned this is one of the most important matters that we could be discussing.
I am sure the minister himself was rather worried that this legislation would slip through quickly, because when he brought it in it was accompanied by the usual press agency fanfare and clever public relations that accompanies most of the government's legislation. I am sure the minister was afraid that this legislation would slip through very quickly before the country had a chance to examine it and see just what its ramifications were.
Those of us who are raising this matter are doing so because we have received hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of requests from old age pensioners who write the most pathetic letters, literally pleading almost on their knees, for something to be done to relieve the conditions and circumstances in which they find themselves. We are not going to let this measure pass quickly without using it as a vehicle to place on the record the plight of these people and as an opportunity to make clear the cynical and callous attitude that many members on the government side are taking in this area. I am not suggesting that all members on the government side are adopting this attitude, but it is strange that what we hear behind the curtains never appears on the record and that many members who tell us of their desire to take positive action in this field are, with one or two exceptions, very quiet when the opportunity occurs to make their views known in

public. As the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said, this whole approach to old age pensions is not an isolated one on the part of this government. It is a typical approach, it seems to me, in handling various pieces of legislation.
The attitude of the government is always: Let us do the bare minimum that we can get away with. Let us never under any circumstances take a subject and treat it adequately and completely. I think, for example, of the field of higher education and even the small gesture of scholarships and bursaries. I think of the election promises of various Liberal candidates of 10,000 scholarships of $1,000 each year. That was the bare minimum. Others went further and talked about bursaries and aid to higher education. A measure was proposed which, although it was recognized as partly beneficial, was the worst kind of aid that could be given to students. It proposes a $4,000 loan to single students and $8,000 to married students. This represents a tremendously progressive and liberal way of assisting students in obtaining higher education.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
For example, let us take the manpower training program which for the past decade has been progressively neglectful. The root of our strike problem is the failure of this government and of some of its predecessors to try to deal adequately with manpower training. Another example is that trade adjustment legislation for which we have pleaded for years. All we got was the usual half measure in the form of the United States auto pact agreement. Another example is housing. In the last few years we have pleaded for an adequate housing program but as usual only half measures were taken.
We can consider almost any area in which this house has acted since the present government took office and all we will find is a psychology of half measures. Never has this government dealt adequately with any measure.
It seems to me that this attitude is being repeated here. As I said at the beginning, we intend to discuss this measure as long as we please. If you want to call it a filibuster you can call it so, but so far as I am concerned I make no apologies for it.
As has already been stated, Mr. Speaker, there are some measures in this bill with which all the opposition parties are in agreement. It is not necessary to repeat them to emphasize those features in the bill which
July 4, 1966

we consider to be an improvement. The government needs no help from us in heaping mountains of praise on itself. The minister and his followers are more than capable in that department.
Our main opposition at this time is twofold. First of all, we have argued that the government is wrong and almost inhumane in its refusal to institute an increase in old age pensions to $100 a month payable at the age of 65. Second, we have maintained and will continue to maintain that the institution of a means test is a retrograde step. I know the soothsayers have changed it to what is called a needs test, but it seems to me that in some ways the needs test is even worse. If it is applied with discretion in a fairly affluent community by skilled social workers, then perhaps it is all right. However, I would enter a caveat and take objection even to this. A needs test means an individual investigation of all the old age pensioners and this, it seems to me, is a retrograde step of the worst kind. I hope the minister will have second thoughts as we proceed with the discussion of this bill in the committee stage and that he will not take this step.
Generations of politicians in Canada, long before I entered this chamber, fought a battle to remove the means test. It was not an easy one.
They were faced with all the time-worn slogans that we have heard from members of the Liberal party in this debate. They were told about all the rich people who did not need the pension and about the hundreds of thousands of old age pensioners who did not need an increase in their pensions. However, over the decades, hon. members in the opposition fought with various governments and finally in 1952 a statute was passed removing the means test requirement on old age pensions. That was a good move. It took place a decade before my election. I am ashamed of being in a chamber in which a proposal is made to apply a means test again because this will do more hurt and humiliate the pensioners than any other possible step we could take.
We have argued that pensions must be raised and that no means test should be attached to them. As I said, Mr. Speaker, various members of the Liberal government-and I emphasize the word "Liberal" -have repeatedly told us that hundreds of thousands of pensioners do not need this money and that it is better spent on those in need. Out of curiosity I placed question No.

Canada Assistance Plan 1743 on the order paper in which I asked for information regarding the breakdown of incomes of Canadians aged 70 and over. I know this information is based on the 1961 census and that the gathering of the information is imperfect. However, I was astonished to find out that there were 433,365 people over 70 with incomes of $1,000 or less. They do not need a means or needs test of any kind. Obviously nobody can live decently on an income of $1,000 a year. The figures I received showed that there were over 158,000 living on less than $1,900. That means that 80 per cent of Canadian taxpayers over 70 years of age are living on incomes of less than $1,900.
Statements have been made by the other side during the debate about all the people over 70 who have incomes of $10,000 a year or more. The return, Mr. Speaker, shows that 1.1 per cent or 8,200 of the people over 70 have incomes of over $10,000 per year, so the suggestions made by the government do not stand up to analysis.
