subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
As my colleague points out, most of those over 70 getting over $10,000 are probably in the Senate anyway.
We do not need a complicated means or needs test to ascertain whether old age pensioners require money. Obviously facts which are known to us prove they do. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) in his contribution to the debate quoted other figures which I had intended to place on the record but will not repeat. They made it abundantly clear that the vast majority of our old age pensioners are living under circumstances of virtual poverty.
What is so annoying about this measure is that in the face of the undisputed and documented knowledge of the conditions of our pensioners, the only solution that the proges-sive, new left, Liberal government has to offer is a social assistance program based on a means test. We will be awaiting with great interest the contribution of the minister when he rises to speak to see why and under what circumstances he justifies this requirement. Our objection is and will continue to be in regard to the institution of the means test.
I wish to come back at this time to what I said at the resolution stage. There have been rumours that the government will take into account the so-called Croll report, the Senate

July 4. 1966
Canada Assistance Plan study on aging. I wish it would. I do not agree with everything in it but I consider it to be a genuine attempt to assess the problems of old people as indivduals, not as an group. It is an attempt to understand what is really involved in being old in this country.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Recommendation No. 2 on page 17 of their report reads as follows:
Any suggestion that these older people, when the $75 pension is not sufficient, should be expected to depend for supplementation on public assistance after a needs test is utterly unacceptable.
I emphasize the words, "utterly unacceptable". I continue the quotation:
Public assistance should, of course, be available to them, as to others in the population, to meet residual needs and to deal with special circumstances, but it is the committee's conviction that main reliance for meeting their ordinary requirements should be on benefits to which they are entitled as a matter of right and that the proportion of older people requiring needs-tested supplementation should be very small at all times.
This is the end of the quotation. It is a very nice bit of grammar and reads well. What it makes clear is that we do not need a means test in Canada in connection with old age assistance. Mention is made in the report of some problems the committee could not solve. There were some recommendations they did not feel they could make. However, one recommendation upon which the committee was clear was that we do not want and do not need a means test for old age pensions in Canada. Yet what have you lifted from the report, if this is where you got it? You have put into your legislation the one thing this exhaustive study said we did not want, the means test. With the best intention in the world, the means test could mean nothing but humiliation for old age pensioners. I am going to read a few of their letters before I sit down.
The one thing that the Croll report emphasizes again and again is the need for older people to have their income as of right. This is something for which they have worked and is something to which they are automatically entitled. It allows people their self-respect and their self-esteem. In many ways this is just as important to them as the actual amount of money itself. With one blow you are going to take this away or at least you are going to try to do so. It is going to take a lot of arguments to convince us that there is justification for this move. It is significant that the voices on the government side that have been raised in support of this measure have been few and have been rarely heard.
IMr. Scott (Danforth).]
I believe this is because in Ottawa we are perhaps removed from the people a bit. We do not look upon groups in our community as anything but distant groups. The old age pensioners, while there are 1,000,000 or 1,-
200,000	of them, are scattered all over the place. They do not have anybody to speak for them. They have no pressure lobbies like agriculture, the unions, industrial people or those who want tariff protection. We look upon them, therefore, as a group on the periphery of our society. We think of them almost in statistical terms.
The only objection we have heard in the house in so far as old age pensioners are concerned is that it costs too much to help these people. There is a new word being used, "priorities", and they are low on the order of priorities. All kinds of things are elevated above the human needs of these people. I suspect this results from the fact that when you get into these ivory towers in Ottawa you tend automatically to lose touch with many of the people you represent. I believe that is what has happened to the Liberal party over the years. You are the people with the managerial expertise and you think in terms of the cash register rather than in terms of the human need involved. This attitude may not even be restricted to hon. members opposite.
It seems to me one of the reasons for the fed-up attitude toward parties and politicians today is the general feeling the people have that we have lost touch with them and that in Ottawa we have governments and perhaps parties that are losing touch with the realities of the country. This is part of the malaise which I think is building up in the country because people like you, with the authority, the power and the right to reach out and touch these people, refuse to act.
If the government even at this late date wished to retreat from its intransigent attitude and take a step that would establish them as a government that cares about the people, I suggest they could epitomize that by increasing the old age pension to $100 per month without the imposition of a means test. We in the opposition would like to do so but the rules prohibit us from so doing. We have used every legitimate means at our disposal to present this point of view. We are powerless. All we can do is plead. You are the people who have the power and the authority to act. Specifically, this power to act rests with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen). He is the man to
July 4, 1966

whom Canadians must look for leadership. We will not get it from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). His sharp thinking has already ruled out this action because it does not fit in with his cash register mentality and that of the majority of the members of cabinet. I see the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) laughing. I suggest to him that this is no laughing matter which we are trying to discuss.

speechtext:
I would not even presume to attempt to move the minister in this field. The government has made it clear over the past several days, as have hon. members opposite, that so far as they are concerned they will not relent on this point. The only hope we have left is to appeal to the minister himself to give some leadership in this field.
As I was saying, we tend to forget the pensioners. We forget who they are and what they are. The Croll report puts it in understandable language. I should like to quote from page 6 where we find Senator Croll's introduction:
Senior citizens are not some indefinable group, separate and apart. They are our mothers and our fathers. They are ourselves in a few years. They are those who have made contributions to society and to our country. They are those who have given their energies, their skills and their children for the good of society. What the senior citizen needs is to retain his earned right in his own world.
It seems to me that this is the type of sentiment from which we are departing in this legislation. We say that, notwithstanding the fact that there are good features in the bill which have been outlined already. When we were discussing the resolution I had a few words to say on my own behalf and that of my party and I tried to point out that I, along with many members who have had to spend a lot of time with old age pensioners, I presume, am ashamed of the way in which we have handled their problems. The Croll report indicates that over 60 per cent of our pensioners live in urban centres. This trend will continue over the years. Before long the vast majority will live in our cities.
Merely to hand out more money to these people, badly as they need it and desperate as they are for income, is not going to solve their problems. Until we are prepared to deal with old age pensioners as a part of the community and not an isolated group that gets a handout every once in a while or that 23033-453a
Canada Assistance Plan we mention in the house from time to time, we are never going to solve their problems. Until we are prepared to deal with them as part of the community we will never solve the dilemma of the old age pensioners. Their problems are the same as most of the problems of the people we represent. They need decent housing at a price or rental they can afford to pay, but we do not give it to them.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
There is an apartment project to house old age pensioners in the constituency which for the moment at least I represent. The tragedy is that the old age pensioners cannot get into it if they receive only the old age pension because the income requirement is too high. Instead they have to live in attic rooms for which they pay $32 a month out their $75, which leaves them with less than a dollar a day to live on and to provide everything they need. I could fill 100 such buildings tomorrow if they were available. We have been asking ever since this government took office for a real housing program for our old age pensioners but nothing has been done. We do not even have a housing program in this country.
Until we deal with the problem of price control for these people, handing them more money, while all right for the moment, is no solution because prices are going up and up and next year the increase will be wiped out. So we are back where we started, with the old fight about the amount.
Until we bring in a genuine medicare scheme to help these people we are not dealing with their problems adequately. Until we begin to think of the old age pensioner as part of the community, as being a person who does not want to be shoved on the sidelines but who wants to feel he is part of life and has a useful part to play and role to perform, with a proper place in the community as a whole, we will never get at the problem of the old age pensioner.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, we discuss this question at length. We know that the government is not going to do anything about it. At least, I think I know they are not, though I would have great respect for the government if they were to provide tomorrow as a minimum gesture an increase in the pension at least to the $100 figure. But let none of us think that by doing this we will really be going very much for these people. They will not live high on the hog on $100 a month.
I do not want to read into the record all of these social agencies reports, which are

July 4, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan stacked almost a mile high and have come in from all over Canada, pointing out the very basic minimum upon which people can be expected to exist. One of these reports was featured in an article in the Toronto Star on October 20, 1965, and was headlined: "Aged Pensioner Says She'll Probably Never Eat Steak Again". The article gives a monthly budget of $126.47 for a man and $118.83 for a woman. It is a very generous budget, I must say.
For example, $31.62 is allotted to food and $41.44 to housing. I defy anyone who comes from an urban area-I am not familiar with the country districts-to show me adequate, decent housing in our cities for $41.44 a month. The budget also allows $6.81 for clothing, $3.29 for home furnishings, $2.17 for transportation in metro, and if the pensioner wants to take a trip 62 cents a month is allocated to transportation outside of metro. These are magnificent and generous figures and are suggested as the minimum on which these people can be expected to exist.
I do not want to have to read into the record, though we may do so as the debate continues, reports from one of the senior citizens committees outlining the plight of these people and their need for better treatment. The really pathetic aspect of the problem of the old age pensioners is the letters received from them in which they tell you what they think and how they feel. I have one here in which a woman comments on the proposed needs or means test, and she says that it would be a very humiliating experience to have to go through. She says that many who really need help would have too much pride and selfrespect to apply, and that is true. This refrain runs through all the mail.
What the government seems to fail to understand is that the older people have a great sense of pride and self-respect and that they will be most reluctant to apply for a means test wherein they would have to subject their affairs to examination, no matter how delicately, graciously and sincerely it is done. I am not saying that the people who do apply will be unnecessarily shy, but a good proportion of them are too proud to apply in the first place. They want to live their lives in dignity and independence, and some will not be prepared to apply. One person went so far as to say that she would even give up her niggardly $75 a month rather than submit to a means test.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we have been pleading with the minister for some days now to reconsider the position and to give the lead which we hope he is capable of giving. Even at this late date when the debate has gone for several days we hope that he will announce that the Liberal party has decided to become a liberal party on this point and that it is not going to return to the retrograde position it has taken in regard to a means test.
I have read the debates over the years in which members fought for the need for its removal. No doubt the removal of the means test which the Liberal party is imposing will be an issue in another election. And let the record be clear that it is the Liberal party that is doing this over the objections of a united opposition. I do not say that they do not have the right to do this. But there have not been to many issues in this parliament on which the opposition has been united and I would have thought, coming as we do from constituencies all over Canada and speaking as we do for more Canadians than are represented in the ranks of the government, that some consideration would have been given to the views of the members of the opposition in this regard.
After all, Mr. Speaker, it is no longer a question of finding the money for these pensioners. That cat was let out of the bag the other day at the hearings of the committee. It is now quite clear that there is enough surplus in the fund to pay the increase, so the government does not even have the money argument any more. The funds are there, the need is there, and all that is required is the decision of the minister and his colleagues to institute this very needed reform.
I wish that we on this side of the house possessed either the logic or the eloquence to move the minister in this regard. I hope he will yet change his mind, will announce that the house will be permitted to vote on the attractive features of the bill, to which we all subscribe and give our support, and that ancillary and supplementary legislation will be brought down-we are prepared to sit here until it is-to increase the basic pension to $100 a month without a means test and to make it available to all old age pensioners over 65.
This, Mr. Speaker, in no way kills the present bill. It in no way takes away from the bill the areas for which there is support. But it would provide an excellent opportunity for this house to do something to benefit not
July 4, 1966

just the old age pensioners. A move in this direction would indicate that we in Ottawa are in touch with the needs, the hopes and the aspirations of all Canadians. We want to take a new approach and to bring about actions in this house that show we care about people rather than about money.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been pleased to note the many expressions of support for the Canada Assistance Plan that have been given by hon. members, including those of the opposition. There are exceptions of course, but it would indeed be difficult for any reasonable person not to support a measure which so obviously brings about needed and significant changes in public welfare legislation.
I have been somewhat concerned, however, with the efforts being made to minimize the importance of this bill. The hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith), for example, has stated that this is purely a tidying-up operation and that there is nothing really new in it. It is true that the legislation does represent in a sense a tidying-up operation since it makes it possible to incorporate the provisions of a variety of federal and provincial programs into one act, and to form the basis for the development of a single, integrated and comprehensive assistance program. In doing so it makes it possible for assistance to be provided under one program for all persons who require it regardless of the particular conditions that have led to their need for such help.
We have come a long way from the days of the English poor law when welfare in parts of Canada was characterized by meagre assistance-the less the better-the placement of indigents in alms-houses, county homes or poor farms, strict residence regulations, grudging acceptance of responsibility for keeping the needy, and an almost total lack of understanding of the causes and effects of poverty. It took time, changes in public attitudes and enlightened leadership to change this approach. It also took federal funds and programs for special groups, developed often in collaboration with the provinces, to improve assistance measures. First came pensions for the aged and then attention to special groups like the blind and disabled and veterans. Statutory payments such as old age security and family allowances, social insurance measures such as unemployment insurance and,
Canada Assistance Plan most recently, the Canada Pension Plan, have also been developed over the years.
Some ten years ago the Unemployment Assistance Act was passed, through which the federal government shared with the provinces and municipalities in the cost of general assistance to the unemployed. This represented a major step forward in providing assistance to the needy and led logically to the Canada Assistance Plan we are studying today.
It is generally recognized now that we have reached the point in Canada where assistance should be based on the fact of need rather than on the cause of need, and that there is no longer justification for setting up special programs to meet the particular needs of various disadvantaged groups. The Canada Assistance Plan provides the basis for a simpler and more efficient means of helping people. At the same time its provisions are sufficiently flexible that special help can be given to persons on the basis of their actual need. Thus it will still be possible to take into account differences between individuals and between various groups of people whose needs vary according to where they live or what are the precipitating causes of their need.
This approach may be characterized as a tidying-up operation, but it is obvious that it introduces a new and important concept, that of basing the amount and type of assistance on actual need and adapting the approach to meet the individual's circumstances.
But the Canada Assistance Plan goes well beyond this because it recognizes that the mere provision of financial assistance in itself is not sufficient. It directs attention to the causes and effects of poverty and provides for measures that will assist people to regain to the fullest possible extent their capacity for self-support. This is not necessarily a new concept, but its recognition in federal legislation and the support given to it is of the greatest significance and will undoubtedly lead to far-reaching developments in the whole field of public welfare. To this extent the Canada Assistance Plan represents an important milestone in the history of public welfare in Canada.
The emphasis the plan gives to preventive and rehabilitative services is in recognition of the fact that for many persons the circumstances that led to their need for assistance could have been and may still be changed to the point where assistance is no longer required. They may suffer from ill health or
7152	COMMONS
Canada Assistance Plan physical disability, in which case medical or physical rehabilitation services are indicated to remove or overcome the limiting condition. It may be lack of skills or training that prevents the individual from securing or retaining employment. This calls for assessment, appropriate training and job placement. It may be family troubles for which skilled counselling and perhaps homemakers' services may be indicated. It may be lack of motivation or loss of the will to work, often a result of prolonged unemployment. Here programs designed to prepare and motivate such persons to take advantage of rehabilitation and training services or other programs designed to keep them in normal employment may be required.
My point is, Mr. Speaker, that the need for financial assistance must in many instances be seen as a result or symptom of problems that can and must be dealt with systematically, effectively and, above all, sympathetically. Dependency is debilitating and often self-perpetuating and, as we all know, tends to be passed on to the children of assistance recipients. From this point of view the provision of financial assistance becomes just one element in the process of helping people rather than, as is often the case at present, the only element. It is a tool to be used when required but used in conjunction with other means of helping the individual to maintain himself and his dependants and then to go on to achieve the maximum degree of self-support of which he is capable.
The Canada Assistance Plan is, then, designed to shift the focus of welfare from relief to prevention and rehabilitation by encouraging, with additional federal funds, development of the wide variety of services which are directed to the achievement of self-support and self-care. Some of these services, of course, now exist in governmental and voluntary agencies and should be more fully utilized.
Federal funds will also help welfare departments and voluntary agencies to engage the additional administrative, professional, clerical and secretarial staff required to extend and improve their administrative procedures and their welfare services.
This social rehabilitation approach is given effect in a number of ways in the Canada Assistance Plan. It appears first in the definition of assistance. While recognizing that basic requirements such as food, shelter, clothing, fuel, utilities, household supplies and personal requirements must be provided,

DEBATES	July 4, 1966
it goes on to list other elements that should be taken into account. Contributions will be made for health care services, for example. While most provinces have developed various measures through which public assistance recipients now receive health care services, it is fair to say that in no province have they been comprehensive while in some they have been very limited.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The scope of the Canada Assistance Plan in relation to health care services for needy persons is very broad. For example, it may include medical and surgical services, nursing, dental and optical care, including dentures and eye-glasses, drugs and prosthetic appliances, the additional funds to be provided by the federal government will make it possible for the provinces to develop and extend health care services beyond the present levels and thereby eliminate some of the exclusions which are now characteristic of many of the programs in the provinces, exclusions which have often caused hardship to individuals.
The definition of assistance also includes welfare services. A useful example of the type of service that may be provided is that of homemaker services. The situation often arises where a mother is removed from her home, perhaps for hospitalization, leaving a husband and children to cope as best they can in her absence. If there are no relatives or close friends to care for the children, the father has the option of staying home from work to look after them or neglecting them in order to retain his job or having them placed by child welfare authorities in foster homes or child welfare institutions. The family can be kept together, however, and the mother's peace of mind and eventual recovery enhanced, by bringing in a homemaker who, in fact, takes the place of the mother during her absence. The father is enabled to keep his job with assurance that his family is being looked after, the mother's recovery is hastened because she is assured that her children are being cared for, and the family is held together.
Let me turn now to the definition of welfare services that appears on page 4 of the bill. Welfare services are defined as services having as their object the lessening or removal of causes and effects of poverty, child neglect or dependence on public assistance. Farther down the page hon. members will note that welfare services can be provided to persons in need or persons who are likely to
July 4, 1966	COMMONS
become persons in need unless welfare services are provided. We are not content, as this definition makes clear, to wait until the problems that the individual or family face become so acute that they are forced to turn to the public authority for financial assistance. Where counselling, homemaker services, referral to appropriate community services and the like are indicated, these can be provided and the will and capacity of the individual can be sustained and strengthened with a view to maintaining his all-important self-dependence.
It has been pointed out by some hon. members that much greater attention needs to be given to the number and quality of staff in the field of welfare. I want to emphasize the fact that tremendous strides have been made in recent years in improving the quality of training for personnel in this field. Emphasis is given in their training to the importance of administering public welfare programs in ways which enhance and protect the rights, self-respect, dignity and independence of people. We have come a long way from the days of the depression when so many people did, in fact, suffer from the attitudes of welfare authorities whose main objective appeared to be to discourage them in every possible way from asking for help when they were unable, because of lack of employment opportunities, to provide for themselves. It is this concern, I believe, which has prompted many people to reject the idea of a needs test, and if that attitude were still in effect I also would be among those who would seek for alternative ways of helping people. But times have changed and attitudes have changed. We recognize the right of people to expect courteous and considerate attention when, usually for reasons beyond their control, they find themselves in need of help.
The Canada Assistance Plan, under the definition of welfare services, makes provision for sharing in the costs of staff training and development and thereby acknowledges in a tangible way the need to provide for adequate numbers of properly qualified people who can administer the programs in ways that will enhance the dignity and self-respect of persons who have every right to expect to be treated in this manner.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker in this debate pointed out many of the attributes of the Canada Assistance Plan and reasons why members should give it their strong and forthright support. I take no great objection to the arguments he advanced, but it seems passing strange to me that the Liberal party which has always held itself out as the party which has endeavoured to do more for the unfortunate of this country should completely ignore and bypass a report prepared by a special committee of the Senate which recommended so much more for this group of citizens, who face real problems because of financial difficulties into which they have been placed by this government.
While I have said that Liberals always hold themselves out as the champions of the downtrodden I must also say that in the field of hospital insurance they managed to accumulate a great deal of mileage because they talked about it from 1919 onwards. Yet it was not until 1957, when the party to which I belong was in power, that it was put into effect. In regard to welfare assistance the

Liberal party is trailing far behind the other parties in the House of Commons today.
The members of the opposition parties have indicated their willingness to give to the older citizens of this nation that which most Canadians believe they should have, a pension of at least $100 a month. There are some who appear to be somewhat concerned about the fact that we did not recess last week end. Generally speaking I am sure that members of parliament went up in the estimation of a great many Canadians because of their willingness to stay here in an endeavour to convince the government that a minimum old age security pension of at least $100 a month is a must. I feel certain that a great many members sitting on the back benches on the government side are as pleased as punch that we are still here today debating this matter, with the hope that the government will move forward with a program to provide this minimum pension for all citizens 65 years oi age and over without a means test. I do not think I need say more on that aspect of the situation.
The leader of our party today performed a job which leaves the remainder of members in our party in a position of having only to agree with his sentiments. He spoke for every member of the official opposition, if not for the members of all opposition parties, as well as for a number of members sitting on the Liberal side of this house. I am sure many of them are dissatisfied with the arrogant attitude adopted by the cabinet ministers in this regard.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
It is my intention this evening to deal with a subject which is not quite as broad as old age assistance and which involves fewer people. The amount of money involved is infinitesimal when compared with the amount that has been paid to date in social welfare and in old age assistance. I refer to the disabled persons allowance. It is my hope that I can convince the minister that the Canada Assistance Plan as constituted will do more harm than good to a great many people who today live in degradation and poverty because the government will not make a move in the right direction. I feel this is particularly upsetting, because there are not enough people in this classification to command the kind of attention that the old age pensioners receive, because of their much greater numbers.
July 4, 1966

I was very pleased to see during the last election campaign that our leader, when outlining the policies which our party would endorse if elected to office, made an unequivocal promise that we would eliminate the means test in so far as the disabled persons allowance and the blind persons allowance were concerned. This meant that any individual who found himself in the unfortunate position of being either blind or disabled would as of right receive $75 a month during the period that he qualified for such allowance, and indeed in most instances for the rest of his life.
I believe there is only one fair way to indicate the great problem that people face when making application for the disabled persons allowance, and that is by reading into the record some of the correspondence that a member has with constituents and cabinet ministers, both federal and provincial. I should first of all like to read a letter written to me by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) on May 25. I had pointed out to him that a certain individual had doctors' reports indicating a significant degree of disability. This man was unemployable and found himself in the position wherein he could qualify for the disabled persons allowance. The minister replied in this way:
As you know, although the federal government shares in the cost of disabled persons allowances, this program is administered by the province which determines eligibility and the rate of payment. After consulting with my departmental officials, I understand that-
-the individual concerned-
-could not meet the definition of total and permanent disability set out in the legislation and the requirement that the applicant be unable to perform activities of normal living, such as feeding, dressing and personal hygiene. It is evident from the medical report that Mr.-
-again referring to this individual-
-condition is controlled by medication and that he is able to undertake activities of daily living.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, if you are alive, if you are breathing, if you are able to move, you cannot qualify for this allowance. That is what the minister is telling me. I say that this kind of legislation has no place in the statute books of this nation. When we reach the point that if you move, you cannot get any assistance, then it is a mighty funny kind of welfare program we are endorsing in this House of Commons today. We talk about assistance. This is the most shocking, degrading type of position in which to put any human being that I could possibly imagine.
Canada Assistance Plan
This is the situation faced by people in this nation who apply for disabled persons allowance. Let me read another letter that I think does a tremendous job of pointing out just how bad this act is, as it stands at the moment. Hon. members opposite talk about the Canada Assistance Plan and what it is going to do for these people. It will do absolutely nothing to improve the situation. As the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) pointed out, the government just introduces a new act and says, "Isn't this a wonderful thing?"

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether my hon. friend would tell me if he is aware that the provisions of the Canada Assistance Plan will remove the necessity for meeting the medical test of total and permanent disability; that under the provisions of this plan his grievance, which I think is a justifiable one, will be removed.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the provisions of the plan proposed today do not meet the situation to which I am referring in the slightest degree. They do not meet it for a number of reasons. The main one is that a person has to pass a needs test in order to qualify for assistance. It does not make any difference whether you are laid out on a bed, incapable of movement; you still have to qualify. It does not make any difference who puts up the money to keep you alive; the government says that you have to pass the test, and if you cannot pass it you will not receive assistance. Let me read what was written about another gentleman. He was known to me for many years. I do not mind putting his name on the record because he is not longer with us. He came to me in August, 1965 and said he had made application for the disabled persons allowance and had been turned down. I received a letter from the Minister of Public Welfare of Nova Scotia informing me that this man applied for the allowance and in September, 1964, was first turned down. I had a great deal of correspondence on this subject and on February 17, 1966, received this letter from his wife:
This is to thank you for your efforts on my husband's behalf re the disability pension. Unfortunately, the day I received word that he would get his cheque in February was the day of his operation and as he never regained consciousness he never knew he finally qualified.
If Blair had received even three or four of these cheques he would have been able to spend these months, at least, feeling a small measure of security which would have lessened his worries to some extent.

July 4, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan
This situation must occur in a great many cases, as I know of a similar one myself. Surely, there must be a way to eliminate a lot of the red tape so that if one is really disabled he could receive help at least within three months after the application has been filed. Perhaps an adjustment can be made so that others may be helped quicker.
I know your letter played a big part in helping Blair get the pension. It was just too bad it took them so long to realize his urgent need. Many thanks for doing what you could for him when he asked for your assistance.
That is an example of the kind of degradation that this legislation, and any legislation that demands a needs test, puts people through. Are we being good Canadians when we ask our fellow citizens to subject themselves to this sort of thing for years and years in order to receive a pittance that is really not enough to survive on, and is only enough to slowly die on; because $75 a month does not really maintain anybody in health and happiness, it just allows one to survive for a certain number of years.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
What else do we do when we put this requirement of a means test on a disabled person's allowance? In effect we say to this person: "You have worked for a great many years and probably you have made some savings. When you have spent your savings on obtaining the medical attention you require, come up to us and we will investigate how you have spent the $3,000 or $4,000 you had saved. We will then give you $75 on which we know you cannot exist." This is what the needs test does to Canadians.
We then hear someone else saying to us: There is nothing wrong in asking people to subject themselves to a needs or a means test; there is a different philosophy in the world today than there was 20 years ago. Apparently, according to some speakers, there is less dignity in the world today. There is only less dignity in the world when you push people down and will not let them up.
If you adopt the attitude which was taken by the Senate committee on aging, you will not subject these people to such a degradation but you will recognize the fact that dignity and pride are necessary to every individual. You will endeavour to maintain these qualities and you will not try to destroy them. In effect we do destroy them when we demand a means or a needs test. Both these tests mean the same thing to every individual who has applied for one of these social assistance schemes.

If the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) is anxious to put forward far-reaching legislation which will maintain the pride and dignity which we desire for all individuals in this nation, he will eliminate the needs or means test from the Canada Assistance Plan and put into effect the system which the Senate committee on aging has recommended. This will eliminate the necessity, to which many Canadians are subjected, of going to the office or home of a member of parliament, of a member of the legislative assembly or of a county councillor and asking him to intercede, in the hope of obtaining some kind of financial assistance which will enable him to survive. If we continue to demand that a means test be made a requirement, we will not move very far ahead of the legislation for the relief for the poor that was so common in the thirties. We will not be progressing and we will continue to subject Canadians to the same humiliations which they have had to suffer in order to get the sustenance of life.
We have to change our philosophy in this respect. The sad thing about this is that I think most hon. members, both on the government side and in the opposition, believe that a change should be brought about. The administration, however, has not yet arrived at this conclusion. The best indication of that is their stubbornness-there is no better word for it-in not bringing forward an increase in the old age security which would be acceptable to every Canadian everywhere. I think any hon. member could go into the street and ask any individual he meets whether he is in favour of immediately increasing old age security by $25 a month, and whether he be a 10 year old boy or an 80 year old man, the reply would be "Yes, we are in agreement".
This measure should have been taken a long time ago because I think that is the way all Canadians think. If the cabinet ministers went back to their constituencies and talked to their supporters a little more often, they would discover that that is the way the average Canadian thinks. The sooner the government eliminates it stubborn attitude in this regard, the sooner the business of this nation will move forward.
I believe members of this parliament have put up with this stubborn arrogance long enough and they will not continue to fool around any longer. We want that increase and we will stay here until we get it. I am all in favour of staying as long as is necessary to get it.

wish to say at the start that, like other members of the party which I represent, I am in support of this bill. However, I want to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that I disagree with the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Groos) who spoke late this afternoon, and I cannot help but believe that we will not have reached the millennium in Canada after this bill is passed and brought into operation. I believe that it will provide services which are long overdue in a number of areas. It is only after this bill is put into operation and after some of the needs for which this bill will provide have been implemented that we will begin to realize how much more remains to be done before we have instituted in this country a really comprehensive social security system about which so many people have talked for many years.
This afternoon I read the speech made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) in introducing this bill. In studying it paragraph by paragraph I realized again that after this bill is implemented we will still be very far from accomplishing the aims which the government has set out for itself in this bill. I will say again that it is my intention to support it and I will list the fields in which the minister has indicated financial assistance will be provided.
They are: people covered by the old age assistance program; people receiving blindness allowances; people receiving disabled persons allowances; needy mothers with dependent children; people receiving assistance in general; people who now receive assistance under the Unemployment Assistance Act; and children in the care of welfare authorities.
This is a good Bill as far as it goes, but it seems to me that when this bill is implemented we will find that we will provide most assistance to people in these categories who reside in the provinces which now have the best programs, that is to say Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. What we are proposing to do in this bill, Mr. Speaker, is no more and no less than help the provinces share the cost. There is no provision in this bill to help the people in the provinces in which public assistance programs have been, and still are, almost totally inadequate. The people in New Brunswick or in the rural areas of my own province of Manitoba are not getting the assistance they should get. If the rates which have been set are inadequate, or if the staff to service their needs is inadequate, as they
DEBATES	7157
Canada Assistance Plan are, then there are no provisions in this bill which will help.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
I am not thinking of a rural area at the moment, Mr. Speaker, I am thinking of a village which happens to be in the constituency of my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in which there is no trained staff, in which the decision as to who gets assistance and how much, is made by members of the local village council. They are estimable people, Mr. Speaker, but they have no qualifications and no training at all. In addition, they are people who, as a result of good health and good fortune have, as our young people would say, got it made themselves. They look down on these people requesting assistance. I have been told by social workers as I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has, that the council looks down upon these people and they are tough with them.
A person really has to crawl on his belly in that village before he can get assistance. There are no provisions in this bill which will help these people at all. I am not going to go into details. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said much better than I could this afternoon that what we need is a national standard. I say again that it is not my intention to vote against this bill. I wonder if the minister has really given any thought to whether the federal government should be giving financial assistance to provinces and municipalities where the standard of assistance given to people who are in need is not adequate? It seems to me it would be a good idea if the federal government, in implementing this program, were to say to the provinces and let the provinces say to the municipalities: There is the Canada Assistance Plan; there is money available from the federal government, but that money is only available if the assistance which you give is sufficient to permit the people who are getting assistance to live with some dignity.
I do not hold any brief for the Manitoba government. Hon. members know it is a Conservative government and that it has a smaller majority this week than it had last week. But the Manitoba government has one of the most constructive programs of any province in Canada for the assistance of the Indian and Metis people who are not living on reserves and who therefore do not come under the jurisdiction of the federal government. However, I have seen how many of
July 4, 1966

Canada Assistance Plan these people live. The way in which they exist is a disgrace to any country as wealthy as this one. I question very much whether the federal government should pay one red cent to Manitoba or any other province for that kind of assistance, until the standard of assistance given is such as would permit these people or any other people who require assistance, to live in some kind of decency.
It so happens that today I received an answer to a question I put on the order paper a month or more ago. It relates to the kind of housing in which the Indians in Canada live, as compared to the rest of the population. Let me just call attention to certain facts. Of the
4,617,000	households in Canada, excluding the Yukon and Northwest Territories and the households of Indians living on reserves, 4,-
600,000	have electricity. When you come to consider the Indians you find that only 12,773 households out of about 60,000 in Canada have electricity. If you look at the problem of running water, you find that of the 4.5 million homes in Canada, 4 million have running water. If you look at the situation with regard to Indians you find that less than 10 per cent of the Indian households have running water, and less than 5 per cent of Indian homes have indoor baths. This is a situation which exists for the descendants of the original inhabitants of this country. I suggest that not only is there nothing in this program to help these people, but there should not be a nickel paid to the provinces until the provinces devise programs which will set standards somewhere close to the standards enjoyed by the rest of the population.
According to the minister, Mr. Speaker, there will be a real effort made to get municipalities to improve the standards of assistance which they now provide. Upon what does the minister base that statement? The fact is that the provinces have not, until now, devised such programs. The fact is that the provinces, in nearly every case, have left assistance to the local governments. This government will be giving a certain amount to the provinces, but the municipalities will administer these programs. This is fine for the urban areas. This may be fine in cities which have full-time welfare departments and which have at least partly trained and qualified staffs to do this job. However, this bill will mean virtually nothing to the people who need assistance and who live in the rural areas of this country, where the kind of program which is required has not even been thought about, let alone instituted. fMr. OrlikowJ
The minister talks about how much better a needs test is than a means test. I am not being critical of the minister when I say this looks and sounds good, but I can tell him that I have had considerably more experience with this question of the needs test as compared to the means test than the minister has. One of the first things which the Conservative government of Manitoba did when it came to power in 1958 was to enact a law called the social allowances act. What Mr. Roblin was proudest of was the fact that in the province of Manitoba, as a result of the social allowances act, the people of Manitoba in 1959 in effect wiped out the means test, substituting for it the magic phrase which years later the Liberal party has come up with-as it does with so many things-namely the needs test.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
I have news for the minister. I would challenge him or his officials to come to Manitoba, where I will be glad to be their guide. After all, there is only one Liberal member from the province of Manitoba. I will take the minister to visit 10 or 20 people who now receive assistance under the social allowances act of Manitoba, which has been in effect since 1959. I will let the minister and his officials ask these people to explain, not the difference in theory or in fine print, but the difference in actual fact between living under the needs test, which has been in existence in Manitoba since 1959, and the means test which existed before then. If the minister does not wish to come with me he could go with the provincial minister of welfare of the province of Manitoba; but I am certain that nine out of 10 of the people the minister or his officials would meet, who receive assistance under the social allowances act and who undergo a needs test instead of a means test, would be unable to explain the difference between the two.
I do not oppose a needs test, though I do not think it is much better than a means test; but when you strip away all the fine language and theory I would suggest to the minister that the people do not know the difference because there really is not any difference. I suggest that most people would consider the two tests exactly the same.
While this bill will mean improvements in the categories listed by the minister, some of which I have already mentioned, it completely ignores two of the major requirements of people who are in need, particularly the older people. It completely ignores the fact that we
July 4, 1966

in Canada-and we all ought to hang our heads in shame for this-have done, I was going to say virtually nothing, but this would be too kind. We have done nothing by way of providing housing for those in need, particularly housing for people who are retired and are now receiving the old age pension.
It is true that in most cities in Canada one can find a few housing projects for people of this type. A month or so ago I was present at the official opening of a very fine housing project in my constituency built under the auspices of the United Church of Canada, named-I am not being critical here-the Fred Douglas Home. Fred Douglas was a leading figure in the United Church in Winnipeg and was also a candidate for the Liberal party during the last two elections in the constituency of Winnipeg South Centre. This project is a very fine one, Mr. Speaker; but if you were to count the units in the city of Winnipeg built under the auspices of the United Church and the Roman Catholic Church, the Lions club, the Kiwanis and the Canadian Legion-and perhaps there are other organizations which have participated which I have not listed-the available units would number merely several hundred, certainly less than a thousand.
When one compares this with the needs of the elderly people who are on low incomes or on pensions in Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal or any other city in Canada, it is apparent that this bill or anything which has been proposed by the government will be of little assistance.
We know from experience that unless this housing problem is solved, no matter how the pension is increased-and I will come to this later-what you are saying to the landlords who rent single rooms to the elderly people of this country, which are very often miserable, shabby and inadequate, is that any increase of $10 or $15 a month is an official notification that now is the time to raise the rents. This is what happens, and the old people have to pay these increased rents because they have nowhere else to go.
There is one other matter of tremendous importance, and this is the need of our elderly people to meet in one way or another their health requirements. In the province of Manitoba there is a provincial medicare program. I am not going to say that this program is of no use at all. Several thousand people have their bills paid by this program, and it is voluntary. Under this voluntary program several very serious shortcomings have already become apparent.
Canada Assistance Plan
First of all, thousands of old people, who could have their medical expenses paid by the provincial medicare plan, do not. This is because having already had to pass through one means test-described as a needs test in Manitoba, though there is really no difference, as I said-in order to receive their pension, they simply refuse to go through what they consider, and what I agree to be, the humiliating experience of another interview with some government official, baring all their problems, expenses and financial resources.
I think in particular of a woman in Winnipeg who was born in the province of Manitoba, has lived in the province all her life and is now 83 years of age. She has no income except the old age pension of $75 a month. When I was talking to her recently she told me that she had to pay her premiums to the Manitoba medical service. I told her she was certainly entitled to have her medical insurance paid by the province under its medicare program. But she told me-and I can understand how she felt-that she suffered one means test in order to get her pension when she was less than 70 years old, and that she had no intention of going through another. So with a total income of $75 a month she pays several dollars a month to cover her medical insurance costs. There is nothing in this program which provides for that type of contingency.
We have a situation in the province of Manitoba where it is possible under the voluntary medicare program-and perhaps on the occasion when we debate the medicare legislation I will bring actual cases to the attention of the house-for a person getting the old age pension of $75 a month to apply for coverage under the provincial medicare plan, and to be turned down on the basis that his or her income is such that he or she is not entitled to assistance from the province.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
This is the kind of program, Mr. Speaker, which under the Canada Assistance Plan it is proposed to subsidize. We are proposing to the provinces that even though they have an inadequate program in any of the categories mentioned, we will pay 50 per cent of the cost. I think that, not only does this not meet the needs of the people who are in need, but it is wrong in principle, as every other hon. member has said during this debate.
The problem ought to be one that sets national standards-minimum standards at least-and which says to the provinces: The

July 4, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan federal government will pay 50 per cent of the cost, provided the provincial programs meet the minimum standards.
I am not suggesting that the standards be the same in all provinces. I am not suggesting that the provinces cannot give more assistance than is envisaged in the program, and I am not suggesting that the federal government in that case will say: We will not pay. I say that the federal government must set standards, just as it will set standards, I hope, in the months to come with respect to the implementation of medicare.
Were the federal government to say to the provinces: "We are prepared to share in the cost of a medical insurance plan for the payment of doctors and other health needs, provided the provincial plan meets certain requirements, namely that it is universal in character, that it is administered by a public agency, that it is portable from province to province," I see no reason why such program should not be adopted, and why such principles and standards should not be set for the provinces.
I want now to deal with a matter that has already been dealt with. I know it shall be repeating what has been said by many speakers, but I want to deal with the specific problem of those who are now receiving old age pensions or old age assistance. I am referring to those people who will never be able to get the extra income that will be available to people who are working, and who will be able to qualify under the provisions of the Canada Pension Plan for certain benefits.
It has been said by members on the government side of the house, by members of the press, by radio and television commentators, that we in this group are filibustering; that we are holding up other hon. members. Well, Mr. Speaker, I was away for several days and am not certain what others have said about this subject. I have no objection to being labelled a participant in a filibuster. I am only sorry for one thing in this debate: I am sorry that the rules of the house prevent our conducting a real filibuster.
I am not different from other hon. members. I have not been able to spend much time in my home city since coming here in 1962. I, in common with other hon. members, was looking forward to spending most of the summer in my home town, in this case Winnipeg. Nevertheless, if I thought that by keeping this house in session all summer we would get an extra $25 a month, which I think is the minimum additional amount that

every person receiving an old age assistance or old age pension should get, I should be very happy to stay here for the rest of the summer.
In a country with the great wealth, tremendous resources and small population that we have, for the government to say that the country cannot afford to give every person now receiving old age pension or old age assistance $100 a month, I think is disgraceful. We are all to blame for that, and we all ought to be ashamed of that.
An organization in the city of Winnipeg which works with elderly people, known as the Age and Opportunity Bureau, has estimated the minimum cost of living in that city. I know that other hon. members have referred to this question as it relates to the cities of Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal. I am concerned with all people across Canada, of course, but I am primarily concerned with the city of Winnipeg, because I represent that city.
The organization in question has estimated-and this was done more than six months ago, and I do not need to tell the Minister of National Health and Welfare that the cost of living has risen very substantially in the last six months-that a single retired person needs a minimum of $111.75 a month to live. I want to tell the minister, in case he does not know, that on such a sum people will not live high off the hog. Here is how the budget is broken down-and I quote from the Winnipeg Tribune of January 25, 1966:
Food, $35.45; clothing $6.45; personal Incidentals, $2.29; household supplies, $1.63; electricity, $2.02; housing, $35; reading material, $1.73; religion, $1.08; recreation, $2.09; transportation $3; entertaining, $1.28, personal allowance, $2.87; replacements, 80 cents; telephone, $3.41; health $12.65.
Let us look at these figures. I wonder how many members of parliament or other people in Canada would like to live on a food budget of $35.45 a month.

speechtext:
I am speaking for myself, but certainly not for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in this respect.
July 4, 1966

Do you want to know how people can live with a food budget of $35.45 a month? This is what is stated in the Tribune article:
Only the cheapest cuts of meat are on the food list. The highest-priced roast is 59 cents a pound.
You could spend a whole day going from supermarket to supermarket in Winnipeg or Ottawa to find any roast selling at 59 cents a pound. Continuing the quotation:
A total of $1.19 a week is allowed for meat, fish and liver. For vegetables, fruits and juices, $2.06 a week is allowed.
Food is recognized as the most flexible item for a person living on a low budget, as compared to housing, for example which is a fixed cost.
Out of a budget of $111.75 a month a person has to spend $35 for housing. I should like the Minister of National Health and Welfare to come to Winnipeg for a couple of days. I shall be glad to take him around the city to show him the kind of accommodation he could get for $35 a month. We certainly would be ashamed to have anybody we know or related to us living under such conditions.
The minimum amount required, then, is $111.75 per month. That is why members of the house from all parties on this side, as well as many members from the other side would like to see, under the provisions of this bill, an immediate increase in the old age pension to $100 a month, and the age at which that is payable to be immediately brought down to age 65. I have heard comments to this effect during this debate, as well as during the session before the election, and during the election campaign. I have heard the argument put forward by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), by the former minister of national health and welfare, by the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) and by other members of the government that, after all, people would be able to get more than $100 under the provisions of this bill if they needed it. The amount mentioned depended on the city in which the statement was made. If it were in one of the big cities it was $125 or $150; if it was made in one of the smaller cities it was $105.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
There have been many stories, I do not know who inspired them, that the minister would get up and make a statement, when he was given an opportunity to speak, about increased pensions. Anyone would think that members have been breaking their necks to prevent the minister from making this important speech which would solve the problems of the needy. We have read stories about an
Canada Assistance Plan announcement to be made by the minister that an extra $30 a month would be available for everybody. Even if this were true it would be a lot less than the $125 the Prime Minister talked about from one end of Canada to the other.
Even if it were true, as I say, it would only, I am told, be true provided the people who are in need agreed to submit themselves to the indignity of a needs test. I am not opposed to some kind of examination, some kind of test, some filling out of a form for supplementary needs. I suppose in our time there will always be some kind of examination in respect of what might be considered luxuries. But I am opposed, and I will always be opposed, to any program by which the older people of this country who have made their contributions in the years during which they worked would have to submit to any kind of test, whether it is called a means test or whether we gild the lily and call it a needs test, before they can get the basic necessities they require.
I have a good deal of respect for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He comes from a region which is one of the have-not areas of this country. Looking through the parliamentary guide I notice that he himself came from a family which had known want in the early days. Surely he does not need any more convincing that the older people of this country will not be living very affluently if they are given a minimum of $100 a month. Surely all the evidence of every interested organization, whether it be the age and opportunity bureau to which I referred earlier, or the Montreal Welfare Council or the Senate sub-committee on aging, points to the conclusion that the payments now being provided for our old people are insufficient and that they ought to be raised, and raised immediately.
I wish to close by adding my words to the words of so many members of this house from every party, including the Conservative party, who have urged the minister to reconsider his adamant position that the present pension of $75 a month shall not be increased except on the basis of a needs test. I hope the minister will announce when he speaks, whenever that may be, that the government has reconsidered and that the legislation will be amended to provide that the pension shall be increased immediately to $100 a month at the age of 65.

Mr. Speaker, nobody will be surprised when I say, like the previous speakers, that I am in favour of the resolution under study. They indicated, however, that they would vote for the resolution, but they spent their time stressing its omissions. I feel personally that it is a good piece of legislation and surely the best on which we shall be called upon to vote.
To hear members of the opposition, the federal treasury is like some manna or an inexhaustible treasure able to meet any requirements and aspirations. But if these members stood by their principles, they would say at the same time how much the measures they propose would cost and what tax increases they would entail for the people. If they were really honest, I think it would be easier for me to appreciate their position.
But it is obviously a good thing to make promises and support popular measures but, on the other hand, the cost involved to implement them is being overlooked and the truth is hidden from the people.
Older people have been mentioned mostly since we started studying this bill. Another measure that needs to be revised has been forgotten, the one concerning family allowances. In the last 13 years, expenses for old age pensions have increased by 150 per cent, whereas, during the same period expenses for family allowances have only increased by 50 per cent.

The government should be more aware of the fact that the measure before us is an important one, not because of what it contains but because of what is omitted from it.
There are very few benefits provided by this legislation which are not already in one way or another being provided by provincial governments. This proposal will bring together many pieces of social legislation which have been enacted by the federal government and will provide enabling legislation for provincial governments, through which they can assist people in fields now participated in by provincial governments.

July 4, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan
As stated by the last speaker, the Liberal party has been very backward in bringing forward legislation with strings attached, making it necessary for provincial governments to provide certain minimum programs before they are acceptable. That is an argument I have listened to with some interest because it has been advanced on many occasions, and has provided something for the Liberal party to hide behind. The Liberal government, in so far as social welfare legislation is concerned, has been a conservative government with a small "c". It has never stepped forward farther than it could step back at the same time. In fact it has often been said that this government has taken two steps backward for every one forward.
Let us consider what was said in this house when the family allowance program was originally introduced. Children in all parts of the country were supposed to be provided with an amount of money sufficient to cover the costs of the basic necessities of life. No suggestion was made at that time that one level of assistance would be provided in one province and another level in another. This type of assistance was to be provided on a universal level in all provinces.
I agree entirely with the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) who said a few minutes ago that in respect of this kind of legislation the government should provide substantive measures allowing all provinces in Canada to take advantage of the federal lead and provide minimum standards throughout the country. It is a shame that people living in the province of Quebec are forced to exist as second-class citizens because of our social welfare legislation. I am sure that in each province in Canada some citizens are second-class because of certain legislative measures. People who live in one province should be in the same position as those who live in others, so far at least as social welfare is concerned.
Obviously it is because of a lack of foresight that this government particularly has been prohibited from adopting certain types of welfare legislation which would set minimum standards for all provinces. I have known our present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) for some time, and I have known something about his background, education and attitude. I have gained this knowledge through talking to him, listening and reading his speeches. He is one of the brighter young members of the Liberal party. Because of the obvious

inadequacies of this Canada Assistance Plan the responsibility for it should remain with some of the minister's colleagues. I am sure the minister asked for a great deal more on behalf of the old pensioners of this country than is being provided by this measure. If that is not true, I am sure he is out of character in presenting and supporting this bill.
Let me indicate my support for what was said by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) when he suggested that the responsibility for this bill must rest with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). Unfortunately, very often when members of parliament discuss legislation placed before them they do so in terms of what it does not provide. There are very few who will disagree with me when I suggest that the terms of the Canada Assistance Plan are such that a large number of people in this country will suffer. Many people have been told for a long period of time that the Canada Assistance Plan would be the Prime Minister's answer to his promise made in Timiskaming to provide $125 per month for those older citizens who are needy. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) may have intended to raise old age assistance from $75 to $125 per month, but of course, as we all know, he is a slow starter. This is the same Liberal government which said a few years ago that a $6 per month increase in old age pensions would bankrupt this country. This is the same government that said because people demanded a $10 per month increase to old age pensions they should get it, whether it would bankrupt the country or not. Apparently this increase has had little effect on the financial resources of Canada.
It makes little difference that the test has been changed from a means test to a needs test. What the old age pensioners of this country need is an increase now. These people need more to live in relative decency, and they need more at this time and not three or four months from now. The Minister of Finance is the individual who has really set the pattern of the Liberal party's approach to old age pensions. Walter Harris started that pattern years ago when he was minister of finance, and it has been followed by successive ministers of finance.
It is interesting to note that the present Minister of National Health and Welfare said that an increase of $25 per month in old age pensions payable at age 65 would cost in the neighbourhood of $800 million. I am not
July 4, 19G6

convinced of that fact; but using the minister's figure one must conclude that our present program is costing us in the neighbourhood of two and a half billion per year, or about one third of our national income. That being the case I am surprised that the Prime Minister would even consider it possible to pay $15 per month. Such a program would cost us in the neighbourhood of $1,600,000,000 in addition to what will be required by this measure.
Surely it is time to stop members of parliament from making speeches such as the one made this afternoon. It was obvious that this speech was written by the officials who now sit in the gallery, and read by the hon. member. Let me suggest that those officials have little understanding of either economics or the needs of people. Certainly they do not have an understanding of those needs and the means of meeting them under our present economic structure. The speech made by the hon. member was very nice, but I felt I should have used the provisions of a standing order to question his right to read it. The thinking displayed by that hon. member is the type engaged in by members of this government. It believes that the establishment is always right, and that if those officials in the gallery say something is true it must be true. The government repeats those truths as gospel. It talks about $85 million being placed into the Canada assistance fund, and how wonderful this is going to be for the one million people who will be assisted in one form or another. If it does, it will amount to $85 a year for each of these one million persons, $7.83 a month or 23 cents a day, provided the provinces decide to pay their 23 cents a day. In other words, the federal government will not be contributing a quart of milk to most of the persons to whom they say they are giving this great deal of assistance. Twenty-three cents a day will constitute an improvement, but there are people in this country who write to their members of parliament-and I am sure the minister receives as many letters as the rest of us-pointing out some of the limitations of the legislation operating in the various provinces. I think the minister would agree with me that it is time we achieved some uniformity in this type of legislation and should be spending a lot more than 23 cents a day on a program for those in need.
