The previous speaker mentioned provincial rights, but there are other rights. We are
Canada Assistance Plan talking about the Canada Assistance Plan and the bringing together of all forms of assistance whereby we can assure that assistance is provided to those persons in need, if the province wishes to put the program into effect. Ontario has done very little in this field.
I refer to the Disabled Persons Act, the mothers allowance, unemployment assistance, children's welfare and assistance, and so on. In each of these cases we leave the final decision not only to the welfare people, but worse, to the small municipalities in communities across the nation. I have often had occasion to speak with clerks of municipalities. In the case of a person obviously not capable of looking after himself or herself, a person who is in need and has a problem that could be met by receiving assistance in one form or another, I am told, "Yes, we agree that this assistance should be granted; but Mrs. Jones is no damned good. She is living part time with somebody else, and we won't give her any welfare."
The fact that she should be assisted for other reasons does not make any difference. The fact that her children are the same as other children who may be in more favourable circumstances morally, but that her children are in less favourable circumstances financially, does not make any difference. I am pleased that in my area there is a large, unorganized block of townships in which assistance is administered by the provincial welfare people and I am quite happy to have as our welfare district administrator a relative of a member of this house. The assistance granted under provincial welfare schemes by qualified people differs radically and is certainly much more humanely administered than the assistance being provided in many instances by municipal councils, who are still going by the old adage that was true some time ago and is becoming less true, that work is good and no work is no good, and if a person is not working, no matter what his reason, he is obviously no good and should not be supported by municipal funds, even if most of the money comes from provincial or federal government sources.
Although this measure is not very satisfactory, in that it does not contain anything for the old age pensioners of this nation, I would be very remiss if I voted against it. The things in this measure are worth while. Certainly, like most Liberal legislation, this measure will be amended in a couple of years because it has not been very well thought out. But there is really nothing new in the
July 4, 1966

Canada Assistance Plan legislation and there is nothing radical about any of the proposals being made. The old age pensioner in this country has not been given any increase, except by those provinces which have had election campaigns recently. I will be interested to know what the minister has to say about the situation in Prince Edward Island, where the old age pensioner had been promised a $25 increase in pension immediately after the election. I wonder whether provincial elections will decide whether an old age pensioner should receive needed assistance.
I am sure that any province of Canada would be stupid to go into an election without promising an increase in the old age pension, but is it not a very odd situation for the federal government to allow the provincial governments to do what we should be doing for the old age pensioners, to decide when it should be done, when federal government money is involved? I believe this is a poor reflection on the responsibilities and powers granted to the federal government many years ago in respect to this kind of legislation. This responsibility and these powers have not been questioned in the field of old age pensions. We have decided, it appears, to renege in this connection and allow the provincial governments to decide haphazardly whether additional assistance shall be provided.
This is one of the few issues over which I should like to see an election. I make no bones about it. If I had the operation of my party there would be a filibuster and all kinds of motions, including motions to kill the measure if necessary. I would have this kind of filibuster because I believe that if an election were called everybody in the country, and this includes the old age pensioner, would know exactly what the situation was and would be able to vote as his conscience dictated. I would be very happy to leave it at that. This obviously will not be the case. However, the old age pensioner has a right to look to the federal government for protection.
In the budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) said that he anticipated an increase in the cost of living of 3i per cent.
I think it is ridiculous, in these circumstances, to say to the old age pensioner: Hold the line at $75. Believe me, most of them live entirely on this $75. It is ridiculous to think that these people can live on $75 a month when the cost of living will increase by 3J per cent. It is not only ridiculous but, yes, it is criminally irresponsible for a government to allow 
the negotiation of contracts that increase the wage structure by 30 per cent and at the same time say to the old age pensioner: Hold the lid on in this regard, you are doing fine on $75.
We should take the problem of the old age pensioner out of politics and apply an escalator clause to the pension. Most of us thought when passing the Canada Pension Plan that an escalator clause should have been included therein. This is the way in which to handle many of the social problems facing Canada. The minister said that it would cost $800 million to increase the old age pension. It is said we would need $2J billion to increase the old age pension, coupled with our other expenditures today. If we were to go back to a recession in this country such as we had in the early 1930's, when our total budget was less than $1 billion, we would immediately as politicians commence a downward movement on the old age pension; every time we found we were in difficulty we would affect the pension by moving it downward dollar by dollar. I believe it is not fair that the senior citizens of this country should find themselves pawns in a political game such as we have been playing ever since 1957 with respect to the old age pension.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
It has been a case of "After you, Alphonse. Elect me and I will give you another $10." We have seen the Liberal party members promising in various constituencies from $46 to $125. It may be fine to have an election every year, because this is the only way in which old age pensioners can ever get a fair deal. If that is the way it has to be, then I am quite prepared to have an election. However it seems silly to spend 10 million or $15 million when we could sit down and intelligently discuss with the finance minister the minimum amount that should be established for the old age pensioners. He could tell us in a straightforward and honest way how we could introduce an escalation provision into the old age pension legislation to take care of the fluctuations in the cost of living. If the cost of living goes down, then obviously the old age pensioner living on a fixed income may find himself the richest man in the country, and those who work eight or ten hours a day would be earning less than he is. It is a fact that there are many Canadians, and there are probably some hon. members in this house, who have worked for less than $75 back in the thirties, and it is not beyond the realm of possibility that the economy of this country may some some day revert to this situation.
July 4. 1966

The government has clearly stated that the basis of our social security system is the old age pension scheme. Our disability pensions, our veterans allowance pensions and all other types of pensions are geared to the calculations on which the old age pension scheme is based. For this reason I believe that the federal government is not being fair and honest with the old age pensioners, for whom they promised to provide in their election campaigns. Their speeches were made up of very confused phrases which may have meant anything, and they continue to be confused. I defy any hon. member in the house to say what is the Liberal policy in relation to old age pensions. One hon. member says the government accepts the resolutions of the special Senate committee on aging and that this plan will provide a varying scale, according to the needs of old age pensioners. Others say that this special piece of legislation will provide a fixed income.
I believe the old age pensioner in Canada should be able to look forward to retirement in some comfort, because of the contribution and efforts he has made in the formation of this country. Our moral attitude has changed, since the days of my great grandfather and grandfather, who felt a moral obligation toward their parents. Today this is nearly impossible, because most young people cannot support themselves let alone support their parents. I believe it would be civilized of us to provide, through our tax structure, the necessary minimum for the elderly people of this nation, to provide them with a decent standard of living which they have so well earned. I do not believe we are now doing this. Those who have to live on old age pensions and on fixed incomes, including those who live on the pensions provided by the Canada Assistance Plan as enumerated in the various clauses of this bill, are not able to live with the minimum comforts they require.
A few moments ago the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) said that if he had to retire on $75 a month he would move into the hills, build himself a log cabin and live on bannocks. Most people do not know how to make bannocks or how to build log cabins, and anyway most people would not like to live in the hills. They could just as well be moved out into the snow and allowed to freeze.
We have reached the stage of affluence in our country which would allow us to provide a decent standard of living for these people. I defy hon. members on the government side, who are so opposed to spending a few days in

Canada Assistance Plan discussing this matter, to stand up and say they represent ridings where there are no people in need. If there are such places, I would like to see them. It is more likely to be true in the riding represented by the hon. member from the west coast who spoke earlier today, where there are more old age pensioners than in other parts of the country because of the temperate climate and other considerations. However, even he will tell you that even living indoors in the rainy weather and sleeping under a lumber pile in good weather costs money.
There are many people in desperate need. I have met many Canadians who have spoken of needs of which most of us probably never think. Some people cannot afford to have their glasses changed to permit them to read or look at television. A few dollars would provide them with this necessity, but unless the Kiwanis or some other organization gives them a donation they are not even able to see what goes on around them.
I will conclude by telling you a story about an old fellow I met in the bush near a little town called Cheminis on the Quebec border in the north end of my riding. I went to see him there, together with a reporter from the Toronto Telegram. This old man was living on an old mine site in a shack in which coal was kept. He was sitting on the porch, rocking. I asked him how he was, to which he replied he was not well and had not been well all winter. I asked him why he did not go to a doctor. He said he could not afford it and besides he had no means of transportation for getting to one. I said "Your days must seem long". He said "Yes, they are very long. I am just sitting here, waiting to die. It cannot come too soon to suit me." The reporter from the Toronto Telegram interviewed this fellow on several occasions and wrote a series of articles about him. Later on he wrote his obituary. It did not take too long for him to die. The reporter was surprised and shocked to find that any man who had lived a fairly extensive life and had travelled over many parts of our nation should finally end his days sitting on the porch, waiting to die, too sick to worry about getting better and too poor to go to a doctor.
When I hear hon. members in this house saying Canada has the best social security system in the world, then I really feel sorry for underdeveloped countries such as Norway, Sweden, Great Britain and France that are worse off than we are. If they are worse off, then we should all be thinking about
July 4, 1966

Canada Assistance Plan getting rid of a few billion dollars worth of arms and setting up a social security program which will be a credit to the Canadian nation. We have worked hard in this country and we have developed as rapidly as we can in our harsh climate, making the best of our abundant resources. I believe it will be a very sad day when a member of this parliament will rise and say that most of the people whom we are supporting under this legislation will have to go to bed in hunger and poverty in a country which, by the government's own admission, has the best social security legislation in the world. If this is true, then I believe the day has arrived when we should really do something about this situation.
I have known some of the Liberal cabinet ministers and backbenchers when they were sitting in opposition. At that time I found them to be as interested as I am in providing social security for the elderly in this country. I am shocked and disappointed to hear them thumping their desks, when they are not providing anything more for those people for whom they were so sorry when they were in opposition. I think if it were not for the fact that the finance minister has said that all our economy would be geared to the $75 a month for old age pensioners, we would hear the backbenchers in the Liberal party demanding a decent standard of living for the elderly, the disabled, the blind and the widows.
* (8:50 p.m.)
Yes, Mr. Speaker, we would hear demands for much of the legislation to which hon. members have referred in relation to child care, nursery care and kindergarten care. Let us at least look at this piece of legislation we have now, under which we can provide an old age pension of at least $100 without a means test. Let me tell you that anyone who needs that money really does not need to explain why he needs it. All you have to do is go to his home and you will understand why he needs it.
I should like to conclude my remarks by giving one illustration of a family that had to meet a needs test. The gentleman of the family, who was badly crippled, lived on a farm all his life. He was the victim of some disease such as poliomyelitis, or some other disease which hunched him away over. He farmed for many years and received a small disability pension. Finally after 40 years he sold the farm, and put a few dollars in the bank for a little bit of furniture. His pension was cut oil and he had to make some repayments to the government.

Finally, this family had $1,200 left in the bank. I went to see them and found they had no food in the house. I asked them why they did not take the $1,200 out of the bank to buy food. The answer I received was that they had been honourable people all their lives; they had worked hard all their lives on a farm which was not particularly good and upon which they had built a nice house. They said they had mortgaged the farm when the children were sick and when they had to goto school. They had worked all their lives to provide themselves with enough money, not to keep them but to bury them in honour. I had never thought about how people who were on welfare paid for a funeral. I know you did not leave them lying around. However, these people wanted to have $1,000 in the bank so that if the woman died first she would get a funeral that would be matched by that of her husband when he died, or vice versa. They had been partners all their lives and they wanted to get the same kind of funeral at the same cost. They wanted to pay for their own funerals with the money for which they had worked all their lives.
Perhaps some people can understand this point of view. I really was not that sympathetic to it. I really thought the welfare people would have allowed them to keep the money, because I could not persuade them to spend the money and go on welfare. I was finally able to convince the welfare people in Ontario to allow these people to go to the funeral parlour and buy a $500 funeral for each one. Then the welfare people would consider this a legitimate expenditure and these people would be able to get enough money to eat. The minister may say, well, there was not any need. I do not know if this situation would meet the needs test or the means test. It certainly indicates to me that any family that had worked hard to provide themselves with decent funerals ought to be allowed to go on welfare. These people really did not have enough money. I think this is the way we should handle welfare. So far as I am concerned this situation indicates the need for establishing the old age pension on a reasonable basis so that people would be enabled to live and die in dignity. Until this is done, I think the rest of the world will look at us and say we have not really accomplished very much during the one hundred years we have been a country.

I wish to make a brief intervention in this debate. It is not my intention to make a comprehensive
July 4, 1966	COMMONS
speech on this matter, although I recognize it as being a very important one. All of us realize that at the moment time is at a premium, and only things of prime importance merit exhaustive study. I do beileve that things of such prime importance as the welfare of Canadians generally and of our older citizens in particular, do merit exhaustive debate if a solution of their plight cannot otherwise be found. It goes without saying, Mr. Speaker, that I concur wholeheartedly with the views expressed by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) this afternoon with regard to the crying need for a significant increase in the old age pension, without a means test. It is not my intention to review or to buttress this argument because I think all reasonable Canadians recognize this is a valid assertion.
The increase in the cost of living has made it impossible for Canadians to live adequately and with any degree of dignity on $75 per month in the many cases where that is the only income. I believe all Canadians have a right to be able to live in dignity in their declining years. I believe all Canadians who are now 65 or over richly deserve this minimum standard because people who are now 70 years of age were in their forties during the depression years, so that the years which should have been most profitable found them unable to advance their economic position sufficiently to provide for their old age and educate their families.
I want to raise a point with the minister which is of special concern to me. The government of Prince Edward Island has recognized what I believe to be a fact, namely that people who are not benefited by the Canada Pension Plan cannot live decently on $75 a month if that is their only income. The government of Prince Edward Island has already undertaken to pay a supplementary benefit of $25 a month to the recipients of old age security pensions. I have been informed that the government of Prince Edward Island-I stand to be corrected on this-has asked the federal government for a list of recipients of old age security in Prince Edward Island but it was not forthcoming. In any case, the government of Prince Edward Island has found it necessary to establish a system of registration for older citizens so they can become eligible for these supplementary payments.

I have looked through this part very carefully and I am most disappointed that no amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act are mentioned. I say this, Mr. Speaker, because there are many cases where war veterans are in receipt of war veterans allowance, and I should like briefly to review the eligibility requirements for veterans to receive war veterans allowance.
From a service point of view, veterans of the Canadian forces are eligible if they served in a theatre of war: or if they are in receipt of a service disability pension or have accepted a commuted pension; or if they served in both world wars and were honourably discharged from the last enlistment in each; or if they served in the United Kingdom during world war I for at least 365 days prior to November 12, 1918, including sailing time between Canada and the United Kingdom.
The theory of the payment of war veterans allowance is that veterans who have done their service are paid war veterans allowance without medical examination at the age of 60 on the presumption-which I think is a good one-that they have been prematurely aged by their service. Therefore, generally speaking they cannot receive both war veterans allowance and old age security at the same time. However, the recipients of war veterans allowance in which I am especially interested are those who receive the maximum allowable under the War Veterans Allowance Act and yet, due to conditions over which they have no control, have extraordinary expenses due to disability, blindness or sickness in

The responsibility for providing this additional security falls either on the municipality or on the provincial governments. But when the municipality, the provincial government, or any welfare organization tries to provide this additional security to the recipient of war veterans allowance in order to make his position in life tolerable, his war veterans allowance is cut down by a similar amount and he is no better off.
It may be argued-and perhaps this is the case-that in the bulk of cases the recipients of war veterans allowance should not be entitled to receive old age security as well. With that I do not argue. But I would argue that there are many cases where under the present ceilings war veterans allowance is not adequate to meet the needs-and I use that word intentionally-of our war veterans. I know of no possible way at the present time in which the provincial government or the municipality concerned can improve the lot of the veteran who is dependant on war veterans allowance. If they give him any assistance his war veterans allowance is reduced by a like amount, because of the fact that these additional payments are reckoned as income.
However, income or revenue which the war veterans allowance recipient may have from other sources is not necessarily calculated as income. As a matter of fact there is a fairly wide range of sources of revenue to the veteran which are not calculated as income.
I should like to quote from a pamphlet produced by the Department of Veterans Affairs and which deals with war veterans allowances. Page 14 refers to exempt income, which is income not calculated in determining whether or not the veteran passes the means test for war veterans allowance.
"Exempt income" means receipts which are not considered when calculating how much allowance may be paid to a recipient. It includes income from the following sources:
(a)	Allowances under the Pension Act and certain other laws for the service of attendants, or for the wear and tear of clothing;
(b)	An additional allowance under the Pension Act for any dependant child or parent of a veteran;
(c)	A pension or grant received in connection with a military decoration;
(d)	Any casual earnings;
(e)	War service gratuities or re-establishment credits paid under the War Service Grants Act;


(f)	Mother's allowance or relief for dependant children paid by a province or municipality;
(g)	Family allowances and youth allowances;
(h)	Bank interest or dividends of $50 or less per year;
(i)	Compensation for maltreatment while a prisoner of war (for a period of two years following payment thereof, after which it is regarded as "personal property");
(j)	Scholarships or bursaries to orphans.
I would suggest most strongly to the minister that this act be amended so that payments under the act in the relatively small number of cases where they might be paid to recipients of war veterans allowance will not be calculated as income. In cases where war veterans allowance is received by war veterans, but because of a combination of unusual circumstances the war veterans allowance is not adequate to give them a reasonable standard of living, a supplementary payment could be made under this act without that payment being calculated as income, thereby causing the war veterans allowance which is paid to be reduced.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter I wish to raise tonight deals with the continuing difficulty that we are having in this country in dealing with the financing of housing expansion. Over the last several months hon. members have continually raised with the government the difficulties which the housing
DEBATES	7177
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion industry is experiencing because of the shortage of mortgage money. We have tried to point out to the government the fact that a good many of our builders are closing down their operations, and that the number of applications for the approval of mortgage loans has been dwindling. Recently I placed a question on the order paper to try to ascertain the number of direct mortgage loans that have been granted in my home area of Toronto. I discovered that six, I think, have been provided during the month of June and five or ten during the month of May.
The whole housing industry in Canada is experiencing at present a very severe drought in the provision of money with which to finance building construction. We have tried, unsuccessfully, to convince the Minister of Labour, who is responsible for C.M.H.C. in the house, that this is a serious problem. He has replied with the usual parade of statistics supplied by his officials, which would seem to indicate that the situation is not at all serious. We have tried to show him the large number of builders from coast to coast who are gradually closing down their operations because they simply cannot finance building any longer.
We suggested to the government that one solution would be for the government to directly enter into the mortgage field, instead of having the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation become a secondary lender who picks up the slack when the conventional lender is not prepared to enter the field. We have suggested that the government become the primary lender. After all it is the government which arbitrarily sets the rate-and I do not quarrel with that-restricting the C.M.H.C. to 6.75 per cent. If the government decides to limit that interest rate, then it should ensure that sufficient funds are available to meet the demand for housing loans. In the last two or three weeks this has become a highly critical problem, certainly in the area which I represent and which many of the members on the government side represent.
Quite frankly, at the present time the conventional lenders are out of the housing field pretty well for the year. Not unwisely, they have diverted their lending facilities to areas of higher yield. They are required to provide the maximum returns to their shareholders, and therefore are naturally going to lend in areas in which they can get maximum returns on their investments. I do not quarrel with this idea, I ask the Minister of Finance
7178	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion (Mr. Sharp) what consideration the government is giving to making it possible for our banks to re-enter the field of housing loans. A few years ago the banks suddenly became very active in this field, and that was most helpful. Lately they have not been interested. What we really need in this country is some assured source of mortgage money.
In the past the government at Ottawa has tended to turn mortgage money on and off like a tap, not to provide housing but to provide employment or to influence the economy up or down. When things begin to slow down the government makes much more money available to make the construction industry boom. When the government feels the economy is becoming overheated, the money supply is turned off. This has a most unsettling effect on the whole housebuilding industry, because we have no real assured source of mortgage funds in Canada. I was interested, therefore in finding out what the government has in mind, if it has anything in mind, which would permit the chartered banks to go back into the field of insured lending under Central Mortgage regulations. After all, the banks cannot lose. Everybody is insured except the poor fellow who buys the house. They really have nothing to lose and everything to gain. Some bankers tell me that these poor, under-nourished banks would be prepared to enter the field. I was wondering what the government had in mind. Mr. Speaker, in his wisdom, ruled my question out of order, but we would be interested, as I am sure would thousands and thousands of builders as well as potential purchasers of homes, in ascertaining what the government intends to do in this field.

speechtext:
On
June 17 I directed a question to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) in his capacity as vice chairman of Treasury Board. The question arose from a series of most disconcerting letters which reached me, as well as every other member, in which a very positive indication is given of a dangerous situation resulting in a serious loss of morale within the civil service. The specific letter which prompted the question came from the central branch of the Canadian Immigration Staff Association, and I quote from that letter:
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The situation being created by this apparent "foot dragging" by the government in concluding these promised pay increases is quickly reaching the critical stage with regard to employee morale.
This was a letter directed to the Minister of Finance and written by D. R. Davies, the representative of the Kitchener branch. In the accompanying brief by Mr. C. A. Edwards, who is chairman of this group, he stresses the following point:
The point has now been reached where the discontent and dissatisfaction expressed by our members in these two categories can no longer be contained and I want to advise you in all seriousness that if the Treasury Board is not prepared to recommend an adequate adjustment forthwith for the employees in these categories then I cannot, as chairman of the staff side conference, be responsible for the crisis that will surely develop. The Treasury Board has the authority to avert such a crisis and I would strongly suggest that you take the necessary action to avert it before it is too late. We are all aware of the pockets of discontent and dissatisfaction that are increasingly appearing throughout the service at various levels. This will surely soon develop into a full scale crisis of unprecedented dimensions unless the Treasury Board stops ignoring these developments and takes the necessary and required action in the form of adequate pay revisions forthwith and without delay.
We are all aware that in the reclassification that has recently taken place in the National
July 4, 1966

Employment Service and in the accompanying examinations for this reclassification, a great deal of uncertainty has been created within that particular division. The basis on which these examinations were conducted is being questioned. The matter of adjustments and the question of review has been left up in the air, and serious dissatisfaction exists within this service.
Last week I had a call from an employee at the central post office in Ottawa who complained about working conditions in that building and asked me to take a look for myself. I availed myself of the opportunity to inspect the premises, and although some of the criticisms made by this employee were borne out by my inspection-the fact that the building was not kept as clean as it might have been, the overcrowding in the building and the poor ventilation of the building-in fairness I think it might be pointed out that perhaps the Post Office Department cannot do a great deal about these matters, with the exception of the cleanliness of the building.
I think that what was probably more significant about my visit was the fact that these are only symptoms of a far more serious situation, which is the loss of morale that is occurring within the civil service because of the refusal of the government to take action and to look into these various complaints that are being brought to its attention.
I received a letter this morning from an officer in the customs and excise branch, and among other things he says:
I expect by this time you will have become aware of the extreme dissatisfaction created amongst federal civil servants by the implementation of the government's reclassification plan.
He goes on:
No doubt others will be writing to you in the same vein, and probably the various branches of the departments concerned will provide you with details of the retrograde steps being taken. Salary cuts, to my mind, are symbolic of depression days, and it is hard to reconcile such acts in times of what our political leaders constantly assure us are "booming". The only boom we have experienced is the one they have lowered on us.
This morning I received a telegram from Mr. John Jackson, the national president of the Customs and Excise Officers Association, in which he says:
At a meeting of branch presidents held in Toronto this week end the Customs and Excise Officers Association protests against the implementation of the classification revision program because, one, we believe classifications should be bargainable, two, salaries should be bargainable and the government has effectively downgraded the salaries of as many as 40 per cent of our members in the administrative support categories; three, we want 23033-455
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion a regulatory group distinct and separate from the clerical group for people performing regulatory functions; four, we want people in holding positions to be able to maintain their standard of living by receiving the full benefits of salary revisions as though classification revision had not taken place until the holding situation is relieved by natural attrition such as staff turnover promotions and retirements; five, we believe that if the salary levels announced for October nineteen sixty-six were effective October nineteen sixty-five the situation would be greatly relieved.
A number of things are evident from these letters, the most serious of all being that the government's refusal to take action may result, if that has not already taken place, in a serious loss of morale in our highly valued civil service.

CANADIAN FLAG-INQUIRY AS TO PROSECUTION FOR DESECRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday I directed a question to the Minister of Justice, asking him if there was any means available which would allow for the prosecution of those who desecrate and/or destroy the Canadian flag and other national symbols. I
July 4, 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion asked this question on the day before Dominion Day, because of the unfortunate incidents which took place on that holiday in 1965. Many hon. members will remember how last year some ungrateful and irresponsible persons in Montreal tore down our flag, ripped it and burned it. Similar incidents have been repeated on too many other occasions. In asking this question I was hoping that the government might give notice of stiff sanctions to those persons who might think of repeating this behaviour.
It appears, Mr. Speaker, that similar demonstrations were planned this year, but they were broken up by the Montreal police before they could start. The Montreal Gazette of July 2, which is this past Saturday, reports as follows:
A highly-organized force of 250 police put a damper on an attempt to stage a parade protesting against Confederation.
Further on it says:
The police took 50 persons into custody as the group did not have a permit.
And further on, still talking about this group:
They were to surround the statute of Sir Georges Etienne-Cartier and denounce him as a traitor to French Canada.
I am not an extreme nationalist, Mr. Speaker. As a matter of fact I favour nationalism only as a means of bringing a more total and more significant contribution to internationalism. I believe that if we are going to make a proper contribution on the international level, then we require a certain national unity and a certain national purpose. National symbols are a means of unifying people. They represent in a graphic way the unified feelings and history of a people. Although the people are free to democratically change their institutions, their laws, and their symbols, they should not be free to blatantly insult and desecrate these institutions and symbols. Such acts only cause unrest, conflict and vengeance. They are not the acts of a civilized and mature society.
Mr. Speaker, I have spoken thus far of those who actually desecrate and insult our national symbols, but I must also mention those who fail adequately to honour them. We have just completed our 99th birthday and celebrated Dominion Day, but how many Canadians took any time to honour their country's institutions and symbols? We set aside only one day in the year for this purpose, yet for many Canadians this seems to be too much. Many of these people will

quickly criticize those who tear and burn our flag, yet they will do very little to honour it. If these Canadians who supposedly support our institutions and our way of life do not show the way by honouring their symbols, then how can they expect to have them honoured by others?
Mr. Speaker, I hope the government will tell us what can and should be done to discipline these people, and if the law does not presently provide any such sanctions, then I hope they will bring forward some legislation to deal with them. I might in this regard refer to Bill C-209 introduced recently by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmo-rency (Mr. Laflamme). This bill would introduce a new section in the Criminal Code which would read as follows:
Every one who fails to pay proper respect to, causes damage to, destroys, alters, defaces, or desecrates the National Flag of Canada or a recognized national symbol of Canada, is guilty of an indictable offence or an offence punishable on summary conviction-
And so on.
Mr. Speaker, we need some law to sanction those who insult our flag and other national symbols. If there is no such law at present, I would strongly recommend Bill C-209-or a similar measure.
